### Row `2DClouds`

### Row `AmbientSound`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `0` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "030993404B0574D8C28CDDA884D6AEBE", "If you want an ambient sound actor to adjust it\'s volume based on if it\'s day or night, or based on the weather state from Ultra Dynamic Weather, there\'s a class included for that.\r\n\r\nIt\'s called \"AmbientSound-Time and Weather Controlled\" and can be found in the Blueprints/Sound folder.\r\n\r\nIt\'s a child of the normal Ambient Sound class, so it works exactly the same. Just with additional logic to control the volume multiplier with time and weather.\r\n\r\nAt the top of the Sound category, you\'ll find the settings for this. There are volume multipliers for day and night, as well as ones for snowy/rainy/no weather. There\'s also a setting called Volume Multiplier Transition Time which controls how long it will take the volume multiplier to change when time/weather triggers a change.\r\n\r\nNote, if you want a more fully featured environment soundscape system closely incorporated with time and weather, with sound occlusion, consider using the Environment Sound system on Ultra Dynamic Weather."))` |

You can find settings specific to the 2D aurora and the way they\'re drawn in the advanced dropdown of the Aurora category."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "ADFA2427465E2D017E90AB95EA9E43D3", "^Volumetric Aurora"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "86F1E6694B4679A133C366A8297C18C8", ">Volumetric Aurora can be selected as a sky mode in Basic Controls. ### Row `BasicControls`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `0` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "EBA7EC9342AB73043B21AD9BFF0A306F", "When you select UDS in your level, the details panel will show the UDS settings, starting with the Basic Controls category.\r\n\r\nThe main things to note in Basic Controls are:"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "6CCFBE09466DC09360E501A8A446D994", ">- [Time_of_Day_;timeofday] is the main control for time on UDS, and by default will determine the position of the sun and the moon.\r\n\r\n- [Sky_Mode;skymode] , [Color_Mode;colormode] , [Project_Mode;projectmode] , and [Feature_Level;featurelevel] , which broadly determine the features and behavior of UDS. See the sections below for information about each.\r\n\r\n- [Cloud_Coverage_;udscloudcoverage] and [Fog;udsfog] , which determine how cloudy the sky is and how foggy the scene will be. Note, if Ultra Dynamic Weather also exists in your level, these values are controlled as part of the weather state, from UDW.\r\n\r\n- Simple adjustments like Saturation, Contrast, Overall Intensity, and Night Brightness. These can be used for basic visual tweaks of the sky and lighting.\r\n\r\n- Lighting Brightness values for Day, Dawn/Dusk, and Night. These can be used to art direct the lighting intensity on the scene, relative to the brightness of the sky colors.\r\n\r\n- Dusk Time and Dawn Time determine the Time of Day values where the sun will cross the horizon. Note, these values won\'t be used if the sun is using Simulate Real Sun. For more information about the [Simulation_;simulation] features, see the section on Simulation."))` |

| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "05363BB144FFAFE6023198896365A17E", "If your level has a global ocean/water level, below which you want to have light imitate the effect of caustic refraction, UDS has a feature for this.\r\n\r\nIn the Water category on UDS, you can enable \"Render Water Caustics\" which will apply a caustic effect to the sun and moon [directional_light_;directionallight] below the height specified by Water Level.\r\n\r\nThe light will also fade down to 0 as the depth below the water reaches Deep Water Falloff, to imitate the effect of direct sunlight being completely occluded deep beneath the surface."))` |

| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "00699315435FF8B18ADE89947FF7B926", "When going up into the [volumetric_cloud_;volumetricclouds] layer you might notice banding/noise or other light artifacts in the volumetric rendering while in the layer.\r\n\r\nThe default settings are optimized to prioritize quality from the ground. Here are a few settings to try adjusting to improve render quality within the layer:"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "B17492924997268C83DC71932410D98C", ">- Increase \"View Sample Count Scale\" This scales the number of samples used in the volumetric rendering. Increasing it will reduce noise in the resolve and can fix some artifacts if pushed high enough. Note that this will increase the performance demand of the clouds proportional to the amount you increase the setting.\r\n\r\n- Reduce \"Tracing Max Distance\". There are two settings for this, one for inside the cloud layer, and one for outside.\r\n\r\n- Adjust \"Close View Sample Ratio\". This controls how view sample count scales with distance through the layer."))` |

### Row `CI_ChangePropertyLatency`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `3` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "956702B54F88B62C31BA41BD20B2C3DA", "If you set an active property on UDS at [runtime,_;runtime] like Sun Light Color for example, you will typically see the change happen over the next 1 to 2 seconds.\r\n\r\nThis is because the blueprint handles recalculating and reapplying active properties as infrequently as it can, caching them and interpolating between cached values on most frames.\r\n\r\nIf you need changes like this to happen instantly, there\'s a few things you can try:"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "4487C7174F00B4D1210DF2B7EA23AAE2", ">- You can call \"Hard Reset Cache\" to have the cache completely reset and apply all new changes at once. If you need a complete refresh instantly, this is the way to do it.\r\n- You can change the max amount of time between cache updates on UDS. That\'s exposed as Max Property Cache Period, in the Scalability/Performance category."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "7A1828254FCEA445DFBD809C1701A672", "Changing a Property at Runtime Takes a Second to Apply")` |

### Row `CI_ChangeStaticProperty`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `3` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "FD7B1BE94F3D70B64FE5B085611F70E1", "Some properties, if you just set them directly at [runtime,_;runtime], will have no effect on what they control. In most cases this would be because they are what the system calls static properties. They are applied when the system starts up, but it doesn\'t waste resources applying them actively since they don\'t typically need to change based on time or weather.\r\n\r\nFor these, you can call one of the Static Properties functions to apply the change.\r\n\r\nFor example, if you wanted to set Sun Softness at runtime, you could set the variable and then call the \"Static Properties - Sun\" function to apply the change."))` |

### Row `CI_LumenUpdateSpeed`

| Field | Type | Value |

| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `3` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "CE4E6AF84A661A94A6555DBDE195B51D", "When the sky changes quickly, due to a fast change of [Time_of_Day_;timeofday] or [Cloud_Coverage;udscloudcoverage] , you might notice the ambient light in the level taking a long time to adapt to that change.\r\n\r\nThis would be an aspect of Lumen, the default global illumination method in new UE5 projects. ### Row `CI_NoWeatherParticles`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `3` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "341E692C4A9C6F2FCC1F5CB486ADA5CC", "If weather particles like rain and snow are not visible in your scene, regardless of the [weather_state;weatherstate] , here are some things to check:"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "F2A551AB4F49D211CBD81993F2EBF6F6", ">- The particle may be blocked by a source of invisible collision in your level, like a volume which has collision configured to block the channel used by weather particles. You can check to see if the particles are being blocked somehow by setting Particle Collision Mode to \"No Collision\" in Shared Particle Settings on UDW.\r\n\r\n- Make sure particle sprites aren\'t being hidden by your editor viewport\'s Show flags. In the Show dropdown there, select Use Defaults.\r\n\r\n- It\'s possible in some rare contexts for the engine to fail compiling the niagara systems for the weather particles when loading them in the first time. To fix for this, open the system asset in the Particles folder (Rain, Snow, Dust) and select Full Rebuild in the Compile dropdown on the main toolbar."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "5306128842B5D05140241EB730FA4632", "Weather Particles Not Visible At All")` |

### Row `CI_Rain/Snow_CollisionIssues`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `3` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "44C8D9024F78BECBBE31939C07B59B92", "If you\'re having trouble with weather  particles not being blocked by objects that they seemingly should, here are a few things to check, based on what you have Particle Collision Mode set to:"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "CDF0A84841D1DEFBAE07D79C2FC7FB09", "^Simple Collision"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "C812F70B48D3498E6CD955B568FB7E59", ">- Make sure the object has simple collision geometry. The traces used by the particles only check for simple collision.\r\n\r\n- Make sure the collision profile of the object is set to block the trace channel selected on UDW as \"Weather Particle Collision Channel\". By default this is Visibility. Also make sure the collision response is Collision Enabled or Query Only, as queries are what niagara particles use.\r\n\r\n- If particles are coming through the roof of a building with a very tall ceiling, it may be that the particles aren\'t checking high enough for the ceiling when they spawn in. You can adjust this distance using \"Ceiling Check Height\" on UDW."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "525E6D1F44842D32425D85AFB0E6F292", "^Distance Field Collision"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "1C33B29640A3D5D0A40891827159255B", ">- Make sure your project is configured to generate mesh distance fields.\r\n\r\n- Use the viewport option Show > Visualize > Global Distance Field, to see the distance field for your level. These are the surfaces weather particles will be sampling. Use this to spot issues with individual meshes\' distance fields.\r\n\r\n- Make sure the meshes you want to block the weather particles have \"Affect Distance Field Lighting\" turned on. This is what causes a mesh to be represented in the global distance field."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "9D4556B843817DB952EFA3850C043CD1", "Weather Particles Not Colliding with Objects")` |

| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "AA076F5C4A9D3D8B645E75BC74218323", "If you notice the color of the sky flickering to pitch black when the camera is moved in certain places in your level, you\'re probably encountering an engine bug with the [sky_atmosphere_;skyatmosphere] system.\r\n\r\nThe issue is caused in some circumstances by the camera going below the \"ground\" defined by the sky atmosphere component.\r\n\r\nThe best solution is to select the Sky Atmosphere component in UDS (found in the component list at the top of the details panel) and move it down to the lowest point in your level, below where the camera can go."))` |

### Row `CI_SpaceLayer`

| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `3` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "E27EAC794CCAE4DCE35C49B2520F3F38", "If the space layer feature on UDS isn\'t rendering anything, the problem is probably the project configuration or platform limitations.\r\n\r\nThe space layer is rendered using dbuffer mesh decals, which are then sampled within the sky material. This is what allows them to be composited correctly, layered within the various elements of the sky mat.\r\n\r\nBecause of this, the space layer requires dbuffer decal rendering to be enabled, in the project settings, and supported by the platform. Note for the mobile renderer there is a separate Mobile DBuffer Decals setting."))` |

| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "A384144C4D8E44233B2941A342EC9969", "In VR / Stereo rendering, you might notice rain splash particles rendering only in one eye.\r\n\r\nThis is an issue with a project setting called Instanced Stereo. It doesn\'t seem to support GPU particles rendering as sprites which use deferred decal materials, which is how the splashes work by default.\r\n\r\nOne thing you can try is changing the Splash Particles Rendering Mode setting on UDW to \"Translucent\". This of course will make the particles subject to the limitations of translucent lighting, but they should render in both eyes of the HMD with instanced stereo."))` |

This is because translucent materials require additional configuration to be blocked by volumetric clouds.\r\n\r\nOn the material, in its Translucency settings, make sure both Apply Fogging and Apply Cloud Fogging are enabled. | `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "50F51EE141F4C3884AF81B8AB5FDB338", "If you have volumetric fog enabled, you might notice pixelation or sample quality artifacts detracting from quality.\r\n\r\nThese are determined by your project\'s scalability settings, they\'re not something UDS takes any control of. ### Row `CI_VolumetricCloudsDark`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `3` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "AD9BE2994493239B509F08AF1C262818", "If the [volumetric_clouds_;volumetricclouds] look strangely dark, the problem is probably the [directional_light_;directionallight] affecting them.\r\n\r\nThis can happen if you\'re using the \"Custom Sun Light Actor\" or \"Custom Moon Light Actor\" option. The built in sun and moon lights have a particular setting customized which you would need to apply to your own light to have them light volumetric clouds well. The setting is \"Cloud Scattered Luminance Scale\". For best results I would suggest copying the exact color from UDS\' directional light components.\r\n\r\nIf you haven\'t selected \"custom actor\", the problem may instead be that you have a directional light actor or component in your level that you haven\'t removed before adding UDS."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "01CFCBEF4953860037C3BD9BF5C6CCCD", "Volumetric Clouds are Too Dark / Gray")` |

### Row `CI_WaterCloudy`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `3` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "7CC18E2F4C4C1943948B3E944A3A2FA3", "If using some types of water or ocean shaders, you might notice in cloudy weather that the sun or moon [directional_lights_;directionallight] appear to affect the material despite being blocked by clouds. This would be because the single layer water shading model tests the intensity and color of the active directional light without factoring in light functions.\r\n\r\nThe cloud shadows on UDS do support the light function atlas, a 2D representation of a light function which single layer water can sample. In your project settings, make sure you turn on \"Single Layer Water Uses Light Function Atlas\". With this enabled, the water should be able to recieve a good approximation of the cloud shadows.\r\n\r\nSimilarly, you might notice the sun reflection when near sunset/sunrise not matching well with the cloud coverage which should be blocking it. In that case, try enabling \"Correct Specular Scale For Low Angle Cloud Shadows\" in the Cloud Shadows category on UDS."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "E248359746FC9E69ACDFA695EFD3819F", "Water/Ocean Shader Lights Incorrectly in Cloudy Weather")` |
| `Keywords_8_5ACC585649ABDE1192D0EAB5258A2665` | `TArray` | `("water","ocean","water shader","ocean shader","water material","ocean material","bright water","bright ocean")` |
| `SubCategoryHeading_15_F6EBA06941D30788CC14989999E6C63B` | `bool` | `False` |

### Row `CloudMovement`

| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(INVTEXT("The Cloud Movement category contains the settings for how [volumetric_clouds_;volumetricclouds] and [2D_dynamic_clouds_;2ddynamicclouds] will move. You can adjust Cloud Speed and Cloud Direction from here. Note that Cloud Direction will be controlled entirely by UDW if UDW exists in the level, using its wind direction.\r\n\r\nCloud Phase is particularly useful when Cloud Speed is set to 0. When clouds are still, you can use Cloud Phase to fine tune an exact formation of clouds you like.\r\n\r\nRandomize Cloud Formation On Run will start the game with a randomized cloud formation every time, independent of the other movement settings.\r\n\r\nClouds Move With Time of Day is useful for situations where the speed of time can change, to keep cloud movement in sync with time during a short time lapse for example."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "ABD6E32B4EC1A573E7CD4CBCC0E910FB", "Cloud Movement")` |

### Row `CloudShadows`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `0` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "2FA75B574DF303F5E1413595AAE0CC03", "Cloud Shadows will be applied to the directional lights by default, and are compatible with all [sky_modes;skymode] , including the ones without clouds. They can be disabled from the Cloud Shadows category.\r\n\r\nThe Cloud Shadows category is also where you can adjust the intensity and softness of the shadows with cloud coverage. By default, cloud shadows fully occlude the directional light in high coverage, but only partially in low coverage. From here you can also adjust how much directional light is shadowed when Fog or Dust Amount is high.\r\n\r\nIf the sky mode is [volumetric_clouds;volumetricclouds] , then the cloud shadows will be accurate to the 3D layer, so that every cloud in the layer casts its own correct shadow on the scene. For the other sky modes, since they don\'t have clouds which exist in 3D space to cast direct shadows, the speed and scale of the shadows texture is determined by 2D Cloud Shadows Speed and 2D Cloud Shadows Scale."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "601A481840BDBCB10E9CE48E1F8C3C12", "Cloud Shadows")` |

### Row `CloudWisps`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `0` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "A469525243E82E84A13CB7827CF1DE1C", "Cloud Wisps are the layer of static, wispy high altitude clouds, which are rendered on the sky behind every [sky_mode_;skymode] (except Space). You can find the settings for adjusting the appearance of them in the Cloud Wisps category.\r\n\r\nThe cloud wisps work by sampling a grayscale texture and using that to apply a cloud wisp color, which changes with time of day. The opacity of that color is scaled using the Cloud Wisps Opacity settings, one of which is used when [Cloud_Coverage_;udscloudcoverage] is low, and one is used when coverage is high.\r\n\r\nThe texture can be replaced with a custom one with the Cloud Wisps Texture setting. Again, this should be a grayscale texture, as only the R channel will be sampled, to apply the cloud wisps color to the sky."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "4E45511C4FC87C11B58BDEAF4E7CED01", "Cloud Wisps")` |

[Sky_Atmosphere_;skyatmosphere] - The system will use unreal\'s sky atmosphere rendering system to imitate correct atmospheric scattering. The settings for this can be further adjusted from the Sky Atmosphere category.\r\n\r\n2. [Simplified_Color_;simplifiedcolor] - Determines colors in simpler ways, by sampling an atmospheric scattering LUT volume texture for the sun and moon, along with adjustable color values. Cheaper on the material level than the sky atmosphere, and more directly customizable. The color values used by Simplified Color can be changed from the Simplified Color category.\r\n"))` |

### Row `Configs`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `0` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "C6A18E9A420F1D35B68DB1B21C7A0FFA", "It may be useful to save a full configuration of all the settings on UDS (or UDW) for reusing in other levels/projects, or applying at runtime with game events. You can do this using the Configuration Manager. Run the Configuration Manager from the Ultra Dynamic Sky dropdown on the level editor toolbar, or by running the editor utility directly, found in the Blueprints folder."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "FD44A7A1406753163EE28F9D9230056A", "^Using the Configuration Manager"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "D2216F0147978821504C2E8F8F6E8DE5", ">In the configuration manager, you can select your existing saved configurations to apply to your UDS actor. And you can create new configurations using the save button in the bottom right, when no configuration is selected.\r\n\r\nYou will be prompted to name your new configuration and select a place to save it. You can either save to your project files, which will put the new config into the Ultra Dynamic Sky folder in your project. Or you can save to the engine content folder, which will put the config file into an Ultra Dynamic Sky folder there. If the config is saved in the project, it will be accessible only from this project. If the config is saved to the engine, it will be accessible by UDS in any project using that engine version.\r\n\r\nThe version number in the corner of the configuration thumbnails is the version of UDS that configuration was saved with. You can continue to use configurations saved with previous versions, but understand of course they won\'t contain data for variables/features added in later versions. So it may be in your interest to resave them so they contain complete data, depending on how you use them."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "143DD38C4BED6C290E2EF2AA56894165", "^Applying a Configuration at Runtime"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "0BA491254D0C0B0D14AA78AB2CAF4994", ">To apply a configuration to UDS or UDW at [runtime,_;runtime] call the function \"Apply Sky Configuration\" on UDS, or \"Apply Weather Configuration\" on UDW. If you need to apply both sky and weather configs at once, I recommend applying the weather config first."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "551BFB31493731CDA3315291F16B5E8D", "^Configuration Overrides"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "62AB54BB4DDC29CAC4FE068EE8AD9FDB", ">You can also select a configuration asset on UDS or UDW to have the configuration of the actor be controlled directly by a reference to the config asset. This is useful in cases where you have UDS/UDW instances in multiple levels, and you want them to reference a shared configuration asset for their settings.\r\n\r\nThe override options are found in the advanced dropdown of the Basic Controls category on UDS and UDW.\r\n\r\nNote of course that if a config asset is selected for the override, you won\'t be able to change any of the UDS/UDW settings, as they will be controlled by the override.\r\n\r\nAt [runtime_;runtime] the override is applied on startup. Once the game is running, you can still work with the UDS/UDW variables as normal."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "B28ACA544416C8E69BB7E2859437624D", "^Pin a Configuration Button to the Editor Layout"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "5BD980D34CAF65E56A97B9A4E27AED4A", ">If you have several configurations you need to swap between while working on a level, there is an editor utility to help with this. The Configuration Buttons utility can be found in the Ultra Dynamic Sky dropdown on the level editor toolbar.\r\n\r\nIn this compact editor panel, you can add configuration assets as buttons for quick access."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "4627649442215281E21FCA809A7BEE2B", "Saving and Applying Configurations")` |
| `Keywords_8_5ACC585649ABDE1192D0EAB5258A2665` | `TArray` | `("configuration","config","preset","sky","settings","save","load","template")` |

It\'s called UDW_Current_Weather_Display, and it can be found in the widget designer library under Ultra Dynamic Sky Widgets.\r\n\r\nBy default, this widget will represent the current weather as an icon, and it will get the current weather to display using the function \"Get Display Name for Current Weather\". There are [material_functions_;materialfunction] intended to help with this:"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "14923F3A40A387D935629DB9B6E39971", "***"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "A80CFE024935CFE2959C37929AACC646", "^Sample UDW Material State"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "68931AA742B3A3FD173CB2A14D4A1A36", ">This function gets the values for material snow coverage, material dust coverage, and material wetness. It also applies the effects of [Weather_Override_Volumes_;weatheroverridevolume] and the [Weather_Mask_;weathermask] to these values, the same way the weather effects functions do by default."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "7E526D4C4623B6EE3DC2E9ACE7D18592", "^Sample UDW Seasons"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "DD56440648A1B8EED5F6F1961599FDAA", ">This function outputs a 0-1 value for each season. As the [season_;season] value changes on UDW, each of these four values will peak at 1. The four values will always total 1. ### Row `CustomWeatherBehavior`

| Field | Type | Value |

| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `1` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "F23440D8485785E49981FAB9C35CFE04", "The [Weather_Settings_Presets_;weatherpreset] have a framework for adding additional custom blueprint logic on individual weather presets.\r\n\r\nThe UDS_Weather_Settings data asset class has a function on it called Custom Weather Behavior. You can create a child of the UDS_Weather_Settings class and override that function to add your own custom weather logic. Data assets you create using that child class will make use of that custom logic. The parent behavior is what applies the Sky Modifier selected on a weather preset, so if using that, make sure to keep the parent logic in your version of the function.\r\n\r\nThe function has an input for Alpha, which represents how much this preset is currently affecting the local weather state on UDW, from a scale of 0-1. The function will be called at [runtime_;runtime] as weather state changes on UDW in any way that involves this settings asset."))` |

### Row `DayNightCycle`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `0` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "C836D827421797758E668C986214489D", "If you want [Time_of_Day_;timeofday] to move forward on its own at [runtime;runtime] , to create a day/night cycle, the place to set that up is the Animate Time of Day category.\r\n\r\nIf Animate Time of Day is enabled there, time will move forward when the level is running. The speed of time will be determined by Day Length and Night Length. These values are in minutes and represent the real time that will pass between sunrise and sunset and vice versa.\r\n\r\nNote, if you have Simulate Real Sun enabled in the Simulation category, the speed time moves is determined by Simulation Speed there, not Day Length and Night Length. For more info about the [simulation_;simulation] features, see the Simulation section in these docs."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "28BA7B5A4152E41AF4D36AAD369A0EFF", "Setting Up a Day/Night Cycle")` |

### Row `DirectionalLights`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `0` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "D495066D418A66D70AA0BB89E476F417", "The [directional_light_;directionallight] components on UDS are called Sun and Moon. Several settings on the directional lights will be controlled by the blueprint, such as light color, intensity, cast shadows, and light source angle. But the rest will be left open for you to edit directly on the component. To do this, just select UDS and find the Sun or Moon in the component list at the top of the details panel. On selecting one, you will see its directional light component settings, the same as the ones on a directional light actor.\r\n\r\nThe exposed settings for UDS\' control of the directional lights can be found in their respective categories in the UDS details: Sun and Moon. Settings which affect both together can be found in the Directional Light category.\r\n\r\nFor information about the positioning and movement of the sun and moon, and their appearance in the sky, see the Sun and Moon section below."))` |

### Row `DLWE`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `1` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "D3A882EC48D6D860EF3F22B64539082E", "Dynamic Landscape Weather Effects is a [material_function_;materialfunction] which can add dynamic snow and dust coverage and wetness/puddles to a landscape (or general ground meshes). The setup process is a little more involved than the basic weather effects functions. You can find a basic example of a material using DLWE in the [UDS_demo_map;demomap] ."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "61C58E604FA258C6FD3B659666D2A163", "^Setup"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "B0B6FF04441AA69ED7B269AA2C641272", ">In your material, search the [material_palette_;materialpalette] for Weather and select Dynamic Landscape Weather Effects V3.\r\n\r\nTypically, you\'ll want to add the function in at the end of the material graph, right before the material result.\r\n\r\nDynamic Landscape Weather Effects V3 uses a material attributes pin for its input and output. This is a pin which combines together all attributes on a material into one. Route your material\'s attributes pin through the DLWE function before it gets to the material result.\r\n\r\nIf your material doesn\'t use a material attributes pin, you can use a Make Material Attributes and Break Material Attributes node before and after the DLWE function to use it in that context.\r\n\r\nPlug static bool nodes into the Apply Snow/Dust and Apply Wetness/Puddles inputs, to enable the effects you need for your project. For example, if you only need puddles, but never snow/dust, you could plug True into Apply Wetness/Puddles and False into Apply Snow/Dust, to reduce the complexity of the material."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "EFDE82B54B9A4BED3DFE16BF8C199C6E", "^Interactions"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "66C635BF4C08418F8B94C88AF9D6FD2A", "> Dynamic Landscape Weather Effects supports any kind of moving actor creating trails in the snow or dust and ripples in the puddles at [runtime;runtime] .\r\n\r\nThe way to do this is using the DLWE Interaction component. This is a scene component which you can parent to any moving component on an actor, or parent to a bone on a skeletal mesh.\r\n\r\nFor example, to make a character leave trails in snow with their feet, you would add a DLWE Interaction component for each foot, one parented to the left foot socket and one on the right foot socket.\r\n\r\nA key setting on the DLWE Interaction component is the Size. This determines both how far from the component interaction effects will be caused, and how big those effects will be. The Size should match the general diameter of the object it represents.\r\n\r\nThe DLWE Interaction component also references a DLWE Interaction Settings asset, which contains the complete configuration of how the interaction component will behave and what effects it will use. You can use the default settings asset or create your own to configure the specifics of interaction behavior."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "0BABDE7440CB1304598582B5F0183D3B", "^Render Target Area"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "089DEA1B4A5297F7240C3BABECA59F40", ">The snow/dust trail interactions can only happen within the space around the player covered by the render target which the trails draw to. The scale of that area can be adjusted on UDW with the setting \"Snow/ Dust Interaction Render Target Area\".\r\n\r\nThe render target will dynamically recenter itself as your player pawn moves through the level. If you want this recentering to be based on a different location, you can do that. In UDW\'s Basic Controls, the setting is Control Point Location Source. This also affects how weather is changed by [Weather_Override_Volumes;weatheroverridevolume] . By default the player pawn location is used, and should be a good fit for most projects. But you can change this to use the player camera location, or to control it manually using a vector variable."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "39B5C8E44F26F5A8B1CF70893EA6F318", "^Nanite Tessellation"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "21CCCE474A957FDDA67FB7B15BF8338A", ">DLWE has support for using nanite tessellation for the snow/dust depth on nanite landscapes.\r\n\r\nMake sure your project has nanite tessellation enabled. Then, you\'ll then need to enable it on your material. Check \"Enable Tessellation\". Make sure you have also enabled Nanite on your landscape actor and built its nanite mesh.\r\n\r\nFrom the DLWE node in your material, plug a static bool of True into the input \"For Nanite Tessellation\". The inputs \"Nanite Tessellation Magnitude\" and \"Nanite Tessellation Center\" should be set to match your material\'s tessellation settings.\r\n\r\nIf you\'re setting up a landscape material without existing displacement, I recommend using a Magnitude of 1 and a Center of 0.\r\n\r\nIf you do have existing Displacement for the underlying surface, note the input \"Displacement Input is World Scale\". This determines how the displacement input is interpreted. By default it is true, which means the displacement input is a world scale value, scaled and offset by the function to maintain that world scale. If you already have your displacement working the way you want, you can plug False into \"Displacement Input is World Scale\" to keep the function from modifying it."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "E88FE03F49D920CD5DE3E9A7B72F3E84", "^Blocking Interaction Effects with Physical Materials"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "67797A7E468807F0FED79A98957576EC", ">It might be necessary to keep interaction sound effects and particles from happening on certain surfaces. For example if you have your own material logic masking the effect coverage. You can use physical materials to do this. Find the arrays on UDW, in the advanced dropdown of the DLWE category, called \"Physical Materials Which Disable Snow/ Dust Sounds And Particles\" and \"Physical Materials Which Disable Puddle Sounds And Particles\". Any phys mats in these arrays will be blocked from causing interaction effects."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "88866AFA4FD4E40CFCF73ABF7160F2C3", "^Using DLWE on Non Landscape Meshes"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "EC830A1C441D04F69FB9ADB4A0589C45", ">The effects are designed primarily for landscapes, but you can use them on a static mesh as well. To tell UDW and the Interaction components what surfaces the components should respond to (other than landscape actors) you\'ll need to add physical materials to an array in the DLWE Interaction Settings asset selected on the interaction component. The array is called \"Physical Materials which Enable DLWE Interactions on Non-Landscapes\". Make sure your static meshes are using physmats in that array, and the DLWE Interaction components will respond to their collision as they do to landscapes."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "5FC756C04C8507A197EA02B1E719B7EB", "^Virtual Shadow Maps"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "3F6BCE0E4C2484601BA14F84CE9D81B3", ">If your project uses virtual shadow maps, be sure to address how the landscape material will affect shadow map caching. I would recommend setting the landscape\'s \"Shadow Cache Invalidation Behavior\" to Rigid, to keep the WPO and Pixel Depth Offset used for the snow depth from constantly invalidating shadows."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "E4A5348045875AA1698C81940C051959", "Dynamic Landscape Weather Effects")` |

### Row `DrippingMeshParticles`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `1` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "42CBF3E0405B5E5F66220F8C46C3079E", "There are niagara systems included which can make a static mesh or a skeletal mesh spawn drip particles on the mesh surface, in response to the amount of rain or material wetness of the [weather_state;weatherstate] .\r\n\r\nThe niagara system assets can be found in Particles/Standalone.\r\n\r\nThe systems are configured to use the mesh of their attach parent. So to add the effect to a static mesh, simply add a niagara component using the Dripping Static Mesh system as a child of the static mesh component you want to spawn drips. Do the same for a skeletal mesh component, but using the Dripping Skeletal Mesh system.\r\n\r\nUser parameters on the niagara component are exposed to scale the lifetime of the drip particles, change the max spawn rate, and adjust the fraction of the spawn rate to use when raining, wet, or independent of weather state.\r\n\r\nThe appearance of the drip particles (sprite size, color, alpha) is controlled using the settings on UDW for rain particles.\r\n\r\nNote, if you use one of these systems on an actor which has an Actor Weather Status component, the actor\'s local status will be used to drive the amount of drips, rather than simply using the weather state from UDW."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "3823D3C141ED2E80DCC312AB5177A376", "Dripping Mesh Particles")` |
| `Keywords_8_5ACC585649ABDE1192D0EAB5258A2665` | `TArray` | `("dripping","drips","droplets","mesh","skeletal mesh","drip")` |

### Row `DustParticles`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `1` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "3AFB16E64DCAD6841201C1AA2660B258", "The Dust Particles category on UDW is where you can toggle or adjust the effect of dust/sand particles moving through the air, controlled by the Dust value in the current [weather_state.;weatherstate]\r\n\r\nThe are settings to control the scale, color, alpha, and max number of dust particles which can be spawned around the camera.\r\n\r\nSee the Shared Particle Settings category for settings which control particle collision and spawning behavior, shared by the other weather particle systems."))` |

### Row `EnvironmentSound`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `1` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "BDEA9C8C46E15997955862A55A2A9109", "In addition to the weather sounds, UDW has a system for playing environment sounds. This would be for general ambient audio in the outdoor environment like birds, insects, city sounds, etc.\r\n\r\nThese environment sounds can be authored to respond to changes in time of day and weather. The environment sounds will also respond to the sound occlusion, which makes sounds muffled/quiet in interiors.\r\n\r\nAn environment sound asset can be selected in the Sound Effects category on UDW. There is an example included for forest ambience, but the system is built for you to author new ones with your own sounds."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "7112FBE949405B397E29D8978D7DD413", "***"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "D2A8A5BF46B852B46BDF9D91C5053601", "^Making an Environment Sound Asset"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "103F68C74D613D11D976988B53D76BC6", "> Environment Sounds exist as data assets, of the type UDS_Environment_Sound. You can make a new one by making a new data asset from the content browser and selecting that class.\r\n\r\nThe data asset mainly serves to point to the metasound source asset which is what will be played for this environment sound. It also has settings to scale the volume, and parameter overrides for the metasound source."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "1E58ACAB48BDCBC5BEA54A95A8EED0BB", "***"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "E724F86444DD7FB528A1C7B8C9A52A24", "^Making a Metasound Source Asset for Environment Sound"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "8AEBC2A24824CA66475C74A401259F07", "> The metasound source asset you make for environment sound needs to be authored in some specific ways.\r\n\r\nIf you want your source to be affected by sound occlusion and four directional channel stereo panning, the output format must be 5.1. The six channels output are interpreted by the UDW weather sound mixer like this:\r\n\r\nFront Left (0) - Directional audio from -X\r\nFront Right (1) - Directional audio from +X\r\nFront Center (2) - Directional audio from -Y\r\nLow Frequency (3) - Directional audio from +Y\r\nSide Left (4) - Global audio left channel\r\nSide Right (5) - Global audio right channel\r\n\r\nThe directional audio is stereo panned based on the listener orientation, and is occluded based on directional occlusion. The global audio is used as stereo sound directly, and occluded by global occlusion.\r\n\r\nThe sound should also be configured to output to the audio bus used for weather sound. In Source settings, make sure Enable Bus Sends is true, and Enable Base Submix is disabled. Then add a Post-Effect Bus Send which outputs to the audio bus \"UDS_Weather_AudioBus\"."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "B63137254E4F3CF34C15A7BCD4E3ADFC", "***"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "116957AE4835FBBB4F938BB6A93E0C1F", "^Controlling Your Metasound Source with Time/Weather"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "60F8E0B24724212E57C61AADBBE46934", ">To have your metasound logic respond to the state of UDS and UDW, there are 5 input parameters it should have, which UDW will handle setting. Three integer parameters, called Time, Weather, and Wind. And also two time parameters called Weather Interp and Time Interp.\r\n\r\nThere are metasound nodes included called UDS_TimeWeather_VolumeManager and UDS_DayNight_VolumeManager. These take in the input parameters above and use them to output a changing volume value, using array inputs which define what the volume for a sound should be in different times/weathers/wind levels.\r\n\r\nI\'d recommend looking at included Forest Example metasound source to see how this is intended to be set up."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "A73B49E546B7D6D5B1F23B9F0B796A5F", "***"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "FF81CF574E04122F09503EBEF98CB3A9", "^Controlling Environment Sounds at Runtime"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "4DA690D2417A8C3F206060B54C70B27C", ">Selecting an Environment Sound on UDW will set what sound is active on begin play. If you need to change the environment sound to another at runtime, you can by calling the function Change Environment Sound on UDW.\r\n\r\nYou can use this to start an environment sound when none is playing, change from an active one to another, or stop environment sounds by calling it with no environment sound asset selected."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "F015F2A6464813B710643AB7D77DF586", "Environment Sound")` |
| `Keywords_8_5ACC585649ABDE1192D0EAB5258A2665` | `TArray` | `("environment sound","ambient sound","soundscape","background","environmental","ambient audio")` |

### Row `Exposure`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `0` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "B0186D6C49151FE0A1FD709CD50A12E5", "By default, UDS applies [auto_exposure_;exposure] settings. Auto exposure is what allows the brightness of the image to adapt to the light level of the scene automatically. Some features in Unreal Engine occasionally refer to auto exposure as \"eye adaptation\".\r\n\r\nThese auto exposure settings can be adjusted, or disabled, from the Exposure category.\r\n\r\nWhen Apply Exposure Settings is enabled, UDS will control these specific settings for exposure:"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "FDD6334F4C7DF9A8D887BAA0887897CA", ">- Exposure Compensation Curve, which pushes image brightness higher or lower based on the general level of light in the image.\r\n- Exposure Compensation, controlled on UDS by the Exposure Bias settings for different time and weather scenarios. This can allow you to specifically make nighttime exposure brighter, or cloudy exposure darker, for example.\r\n- Metering Mode, exposed as Exposure Metering Mode. This controls if auto exposure is applied, and which type. You can change UDS\' exposure settings to Manual as well. This would disable auto exposure, but still allow using the exposure bias settings.\r\n- MinEV100 and MaxEV100, which control the range of brightness that auto exposure will try to adapt to. This is controlled on UDS with the Exposure Brightness Range setting."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "3FF6D5C941DF511630A11CA6971C0FB5", "If you\'re trying to fine tune auto exposure behavior with these settings and/or the additional exposure settings in a post process volume or camera, I\'d recommend using the viewport view mode found in Show > Visualize > HDR(Eye Adaptation) to see exactly what auto exposure is doing behind the scenes."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "33002F914900A8329D5503A1D2E50325", "Exposure")` |
| `Keywords_8_5ACC585649ABDE1192D0EAB5258A2665` | `TArray` | `("exposure","auto exposure","eye adaptation")` |

### Row `FeatureLevel`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `0` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "E57B0F9D47ED675DF41443849076BB0A", "[Feature_Level_;featurelevel] is a setting in Basic Controls on UDS. This should be set to match the targeted rendering feature level for your project. For example, if you\'re building for the mobile renderer, you should be sure to change Feature Level over to Mobile.\r\n\r\nFeature Level will be used by the system to correct for limitations of the selected level. For example, if mobile is selected, incompatible [Sky_Modes_;skymode] like [Volumetric_Clouds_;volumetricclouds] and [Volumetric_Aurora_;volumetricaurora] will be replaced with compatible modes. The modes used as replacements are exposed to the user in the Mobile category.\r\n\r\nIf you are building your project for devices across multiple feature levels, you can have UDS set its feature level based on the Platform Name on startup. The option for that is found in the Mobile category."))` |

|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `0` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "DEDB98ED4B5A6F5D06A7039CCE7CACFB", "The Fog Color category is where the settings for the color of the [height_fog_;heightfog] are, but how they\'re used by UDS depends heavily on the project setting \"Support Sky Atmosphere Affecting Height Fog\".\r\n\r\nThis setting should typically be enabled by default in new projects, and I would recommend leaving it enabled, as it derives colors for fog directly from the sky atmosphere, and this usually produces good, desired results. If this project setting is on, only some of the Fog Color settings on UDS will be used by the fog during most circumstances, as the sky atmosphere will be used for fog color directly instead.\r\n\r\nIf you want more direct control over fog color on its own however, you might try disabling that project setting, to allow the fog to always use the Fog Color settings alone to determine fog colors.\r\n\r\nNote, you can disregard everything above if you are using the [Simplified_Color_;simplifiedcolor] option for [Color_Mode;colormode] , as the sky atmosphere is not enabled at all in that mode. If Simplified Color is selected, all the Fog Color settings will be used by the fog."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "4DB2E0B3422159E9A2094B802E2C1CD4", "Fog Color")` |
| `Keywords_8_5ACC585649ABDE1192D0EAB5258A2665` | `TArray` | `("fog color","fog","fog brightness","color","inscattering","atmosphere","mist")` |

### Row `FogDensity`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `0` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "011F5AA54246C544D95ADD94313C2E81", "The Fog Density category on UDS is where variables like [Cloud_Coverage_;udscloudcoverage] and [Fog_;udsfog] are used to determine the density, height falloff, and start distance of the [exponential_height_fog_;heightfog] layer.\r\n\r\nDensity is how thick/opaque the fog will be with distance from the camera. Height Falloff is how quickly fog density dissipates above the height of the fog component.\r\n\r\nFor density, there is a base value, and then values added to density for Cloud Coverage, Fog, and Dust Amount.\r\n\r\nFor height falloff, there is a base value, and then falloff values for a cloudy, foggy, and dusty state, which are used directly, not added together.\r\n\r\nThe start distance of the fog is derived from the density, using a value for start distance at low density, and a density value where start distance will be reduced to 0, to allow fog right next to the camera."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "B5D4584C4936591B39C96C8B629D8D0F", "Fog Density")` |
| `Keywords_8_5ACC585649ABDE1192D0EAB5258A2665` | `TArray` | `("fog density","height fog","fog","mist")` |
| `SubCategoryHeading_15_F6EBA06941D30788CC14989999E6C63B` | `bool` | `False` |
| `SuggestedEntries_19_9776F58E45A513F145D90BBE28516AA1` | `TArray` | `("VolumetricFog")` |

### Row `FoliageWindMovement`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `1` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "27D944644619083494CC688F7B56185E", "Foliage Wind Movement is a [material_function_;materialfunction] which outputs world position offset to add simple noise based movement to a material, based on the wind intensity and direction on UDW. It\'s intended primarily for foliage models.\r\n\r\nNote, if working with foliage models which have their own wind movement setup already, it may be a better and simpler option to just modify those existing wind effects to reference the state of UDW\'s wind instead. You can use the Sample UDW Wind function to get parameters for the wind state and use those values to replace the parameters used by the existing effects."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "F46A63F3468F7A340AED58ABC059B34C", "***"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "4D182475498D26A782560E9CDA1822C5", "^Wind Movement Overview"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "262226324BF9A29DF6F7B481D4771C00", ">The movement generated by the function is split into three layers:\r\n\r\n- Small Movement is a high frequency layer for features like leaves, grass blades, and the ends of branches.\r\n\r\n- Medium Movement is a middle frequency layer made to affect larger features like whole branches.\r\n\r\n- Large Movement is a low frequency swaying movement which bends the entire mesh with gusts of the wind.\r\n\r\nAll three are enabled by default, but they can be individually disabled using the Apply inputs on the function."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "B6EACA1145E5BB031C1372B3E41DC767", "^Masking Movement Layers"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "D890DB024A4299C219BEC393CF424F81", ">Each of the three movement layers has an input to mask the layer. This is a value from 0-1, multiplied over the strength of the movement layer.\r\n\r\nTypically, foliage models are authored with vertex color channels for masking levels of movement like this, but there is no common standard for what channel will be used for what kind of information. If you\'re using foliage models you did not author yourself, you\'ll need to take a look at their vertex colors to get an idea of what each channel is used for and how you might apply them to masking the three movement layers.\r\n\r\nThe Small Movement layer is the only one where a mask input is required. The Medium and Large layers will try to generate a simple mask automatically if one isn\'t supplied, using position relative to the mesh\'s pivot, but this auto mask doesn\'t know anything about the structure of the specific model, so a vertex color channel authored for this kind of masking will always be better to use."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "779FBDDC4C9D1E99D259F1A66FF213D6", "***"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "BF0E3BFB49FC745F28AC9BBBC6383CD0", "The inputs for each movement layer can be used to customize the movement logic used for each. When adding this function to a foliage master material, I\'d recommend using parameters for some of these inputs, so you can toggle and adjust the layers used on material instances for specific models/types of foliage."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "944883FD445D548DD73B658179861826", "Foliage Wind Movement")` |
| `Keywords_8_5ACC585649ABDE1192D0EAB5258A2665` | `TArray` | `("wind","foliage","foliage wind movement","foliage wind","wind effect","wind material","material functions","material effects")` |
| `SubCategoryHeading_15_F6EBA06941D30788CC14989999E6C63B` | `bool` | `False` |

### Row `GetTimeofDay`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `0` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "BC90F98D4215BADD9980699B987F2E5B", "To get [Time_of_Day_;timeofday] from UDS, there are several ways you can sample the time in various formats."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "808D42AE4A63660A6F3A99B13A099A54", ">- \"Get Time of Day\" outputs the float value of Time of Day directly, from 0-2400.\r\n\r\n- \"Get Time Code\" will output a Time Code structure, with hours/minutes/seconds values.\r\n\r\n- \"Get Date Time\" will output a Date Time structure, with the time in hours/minutes/seconds as well as the simulation date.\r\n\r\n- \"Is It Daytime?\" will output a boolean which is true if the sun is up. If rather than the specific time you just need to know if it\'s day or not, this function is the one to use."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "816C62A24727577BF50893B8869059A7", "[IMAGE]\r\nhttps://imagedelivery.net/dJ8zT5MNjUXoua7duc582w/0ff03436-7abd-4c82-ebb8-2644978a6c00/public\r\nFour functions for getting the time from Ultra Dynamic Sky"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "9E418B57492891C614C4089D2AA225A6", "For displaying the time on screen in a simple way, UDS comes with two clock widgets. These can be found in the widget designer palette in the Ultra Dynamic Sky Widgets category."))` |

| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "518E8DC346D63367346261979A41B1E0", "Glass Window Rain Drips is a [material_function_;materialfunction] which can add refractive water droplets dripping down a thin glass surface like a window in response to rain on UDW. It is made to be used on translucent materials only."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "B7A4EB06467CB50904BF4889FE27C6E5", "^Setup"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "DE6550C44A0700480516D3AB8CDBDF86", ">To add Glass Window Rain Drips to your material, search the [material_palette_;materialpalette] for Weather and select Glass Window Rain Drips.\r\n\r\nThe material function modifies the Base Color and Opacity, and outputs Base Color, Emissive Color and Opacity. Only input what [attributes_;materialattributes] your material is already using, but make sure to use all three of the outputs for your material result.\r\n\r\nThe UVs used for the drip textures will be simple world space position based UVs by default, but you can replace them using the UVs input. This is recommended if using the material on any kind of moving surface, as world space UVs will not move with the mesh."))` |

| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "0F25FD174A86C81D4E6CFDBB96D82A6B", "From the Heat Distortion category on UDW, you can enable an effect of heat distortion/heat haze. See the entry on the temperature system for details on how temperature is calculated by UDW.\r\n\r\nYou can also manipulate Manual Heat Distortion to add distortion irrespective of the temperature."))` |

### Row `Int_Adj`

| Field | Type | Value |

| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `0` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "EC8CC46A4E550ACAE0E98AA3C7760CBC", "UDS has a category called Interior Adjustments, which if enabled, you can use to adjust a few things like fog and light, based on how occluded the camera is by surrounding scene collision.\r\n\r\nTo use these settings, first check \"Apply Interior Adjustments\" in the Interior Adjustments category. Then, make your changes to the settings below, which modify various properties of the sky when inside an interior.\r\n\r\nSee the Player Occlusion category for the settings which define how the scene is queried to determine the occlusion value used by Interior Adjustments.\r\n\r\nYou can also place the [UDS_Occlusion_Volume_;udsocclusionvolume] actor, found in Blueprints/Occlusion, to force specific spaces to be fully occluded and always apply the interior adjustments. Note the Occlusion Mode setting in the Player Occlusion category, which sets if occlusion is determined by the traces for collision, the occlusion volumes, or both."))` |

### Row `LightComponents`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `0` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "8ED1C4924D5665A9F2A5988F7199EBAA", "UDS has light components for the [directional_lights_;directionallight] and [sky_light;skylight] . The component used for each will be determined by the settings in their respective categories (Sun, Moon, and Sky Light), and in the case of the sky light, the [Sky_Light_Mode_;skylightmode] setting.\r\n\r\nNote that while it\'s possible to have UDS reference a light actor for the sun, moon or sky light, instead of using the built in component, this is not recommended in any situation except those which specifically require a light actor. For example third party assets or plugins may occasionally require a light actor reference. This is really the only situation it should be necessary to use an actor instead of the built in components.\r\n\r\nIf you do have to use light actors in place of the components, note these additional steps:"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "3139D5B442C54644A8EFB4B9C79584D2", ">- For the directional lights, there is a setting on the component called \"Cloud Scattered Luminance Scale\" which controls how the lights affect the clouds. This isn\'t something exposed to blueprint control, so UDS cannot apply it to your light actor itself. You\'ll need to copy the value for Clouds Scattered Luminance Scale from the Sun or Moon component on UDS to your directional light actor.\r\n\r\n- Similarly, on a sky light there is a setting called Source Type which UDS cannot control, but needs to be set in accordance with UDS\' Sky Light Mode setting. For \"Cubemap with Dynamic Color Tinting\" and \"Custom Cubemap\", make sure the Source Type on your sky light actor is Specified Cubemap. For the sky light mode called Capture Based, make sure the source type is set to Captured Scene."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "CAA1066B4397722D722C6DA182D6D5B4", "Light Components")` |
| `Keywords_8_5ACC585649ABDE1192D0EAB5258A2665` | `TArray` | `("lights","light components","components","directional lights","sun","moon","sky light")` |

### Row `Lightning`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `1` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "0FFA93EA467CD4386DD0EF8F732B850C", "There are two types of lightning in UDW. Lightning Flashes and Obscured Lightning. Lightning Flashes are the big lightning bolts which can cast light into the scene and have a directly associated loud crash of thunder. Obscured Lightning is the idle particle effect which looks like flashes of lightning hidden in the cloud layer.\r\n\r\nIn the Lightning category, you can adjust the interval between Lightning Flashes and the frequency of Obscured Lightning. You can adjust or disable the [directional_light_;directionallight] source for Lightning Flashes and the color of the lights and effects. If you\'re looking for settings relating to the thunder sound effects, those are in the Sound Effects category.\r\n\r\nThe amount of lightning of both types will scale with the Thunder/Lightning value of the current [weather_state;weatherstate] ."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "E3EE30F642CD76DE119638BAD74291E9", "^Manually Spawn a Lightning Flash"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "6ABEC2514A79BD517059F8A21B4F22C8", ">If you need to manually trigger a Lightning Flash, you can do this. Call the function Flash Lightning on UDW to spawn a single flash. It has an input to enable a custom lightning location as well. Note that this is the position of the root of the lightning bolt, so it should be at cloud level. If Custom Target Location is a value other than 0, that will be the location the lightning bolt ends at."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "89A2D11440F1023E29AAB5A65AF78C46", "[IMAGE]\r\nhttps://imagedelivery.net/dJ8zT5MNjUXoua7duc582w/51e3c111-13fe-4f7f-55ea-c200bc69bd00/public\r\nCalling the Flash Lightning function, to manually spawn a lightning flash."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "B7F94C304EF7D2657404979D755BC69B", "^Making Random Lightning Flashes Strike Specific Actors"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "03E472A6416F0EF91C538A8FB291406D", "> There is some simple support for making the randomly spawned lightning flashes strike actors in the level.\r\n\r\nTo do this, add the blueprint interface \"UDW_Lightning Strikable Actor Interface\" to your actors. Supply it outputs for the interface function \"Test for Potential Lightning Strike\". This function should output whether the actor can currently be struck by lightning, and the world location where the strike will hit.\r\n\r\nOn UDW, in the Lightning category, toggle on the setting \"Enable Lightning Flashes Striking Actors\" to turn on the logic which checks the level for strikable actors.\r\n\r\nThe setting \"Fraction Of Lightning Flashes Which Can Strike Actors\" controls how many lightning flashes can potentially strike actors, if any are in range.\r\n\r\nThe blueprint interface also has a function \"Struck by Lightning\" which is called by UDW when the actor is struck. You could use it to spawn extra effects or perform game logic when the actor gets struck by lightning."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "66E9B8F04B424B81BB5050882F92B25A", "Lightning")` |
| `Keywords_8_5ACC585649ABDE1192D0EAB5258A2665` | `TArray` | `("lightning","lightning bolt","thunder","lightning flashes","obscured lightning","effects")` |

### Row `LightToggleDayNight`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `0` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "D9FB9DF64925AF61D54774A6BDEFE6A2", "There is a special component included to help make a light which turns on and off at sunset/sunrise. It\'s the \"Light Day-Night Toggle\" component found in the Blueprints/Utilities folder.\r\n\r\nJust add one of these components as a child of any light component on an actor."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "229550CF4068344E993F3F800512E37A", "[IMAGE]\r\nhttps://imagedelivery.net/dJ8zT5MNjUXoua7duc582w/aa80ecf6-5c50-425d-3a42-c8b252537600/public\r\nThe basic intended hierarchy. The toggle component should be parented to the light component to control it."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "6257C18E46DC7F69775C29977238075E", "When the level is played, the light\'s active state will be determined by if the sun is up or not. It will be on at night by default, but you can change that using a setting on the component.\r\n\r\nBy default the light will also animate its intensity as it powers on, to imitate some types of lamps. You can disable this or adjust it from the component\'s settings.\r\n\r\nThe state of the light can also be used to control a \"Light Toggle\" scalar parameter on an array of dynamic material instances. Just add a dynamic material instance to that array, and the parameter (from 0 to 1) will be set as the state of the light changes."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "5F0FEB7940389174965DBC87C42B1194", "If you need to toggle lights which just exist as emissive color in materials (with no light component) there are material functions you can use for that instead of a blueprint approach. The functions \"Day to Night Color\" and \"Day to Night Float\" will switch between two inputs based on if the sun is up or down."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "E355E0CC4F7C6939558EF1914686E57E", "Turning On Lights in Your Level at Night")` |
| `Keywords_8_5ACC585649ABDE1192D0EAB5258A2665` | `TArray` | `("lights","sunset","sunrise","night","day","light")` |
| `SubCategoryHeading_15_F6EBA06941D30788CC14989999E6C63B` | `bool` | `False` |

### Row `LoopingClouds`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `0` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "EC7815D041A2208B0FF8C8A00438DD89", "If you need to make the [volumetric_clouds_;volumetricclouds] seamlessly loop, for rendering a looping movie for example, this is possible within some constraints.\r\n\r\nThe only way for the loop to occur is for the formation texture to make one full 0-1 cycle across its UVs. So the loop is necessarily quite long at a minimum with clouds moving at a normal speed.\r\n\r\nTo configure the clouds to loop seamlessly, follow these steps:\r\n\r\nIn the Cloud Movement category:"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "301630B14B147B55E41D018FC91B942D", ">- Set Cloud Speed to 0. You\'ll be using the Cloud Phase variable to control time within the loop.\r\n- Make sure Cloud Direction is set to be along a single axis (0, 90, 180, or 270)\r\n- Set Formation Change Speed to 1. (Alternatively you could use 0.5, but the loop would need to be twice as long.)"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "4372DE154A8217E97BBA0C8A7BDD2DD1", "In the Volumetric Clouds category:"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "AEEE47AB40BC25B38DF008AC9BD95B9E", ">- Set 3D Noise Scale to 1.\r\n- Set Cloud Formation Texture Scale to 1.\r\n- Set Macro Variation to 0.\r\n- Set 3D Noise Vertical Movement to 0."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "8CCD130140AB6A4D1F457480E89E3FAC", "With this configuration, you can keyframe the Cloud Phase variable from 0-100 to create an animation of cloud movement that loops seamlessly. (If you used Formation Change Speed of 0.5, the loop would be from 0-200 instead.)"))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "8F71D667427358DF8C84FE8CD10AC942", "Looping the Volumetric Cloud Movement")` |
| `Keywords_8_5ACC585649ABDE1192D0EAB5258A2665` | `TArray` | `("loop","looping","clouds","volumetric clouds")` |

### Row `ManualPositionSun`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `0` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "DF3F84DC4972EC04DC1FE9B52C39AE54", "It is possible to disconnect the sun or moon\'s position from time, and place them completely manually.\r\n\r\nTo do this, check Manually Position Sun Target in the Sun category, or Manually Position Moon Target, in the Moon category.\r\n\r\nWith that turned on, find the blue diamond shaped widget labeled Sun Target or Moon Target, visible on the UDS actor when it\'s selected. Select that widget and move it to adjust the position of the sun or moon.\r\n\r\nThe direction of the sun/moon will be determined by the direction from the UDS actor to the position of that target widget."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "22DF3E57429221D8316873B19D69BE75", "[IMAGE]\r\nhttps://imagedelivery.net/dJ8zT5MNjUXoua7duc582w/5753208b-ab33-4a91-7d34-4f015610dd00/public\r\nThe Sun Target widget on UDS, which can be moved to position the sun, when \"Manually Position Sun Target\" is true."))` |

### Row `ManualWeatherState`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `1` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "05AAF0FA4389F52730A8D784651ADC7D", "Much of the weather system is designed around the [weather_preset_assets;weatherpreset] , to simplify controlling the [weather_state._;weatherstate] But you can also control weather state\'s individual values without relying on preset assets. The way to do this is using the [Manual_Weather_State;manualweatherstate] .\r\n\r\nTo do this, first clear the Weather setting in Basic Controls, so no preset asset is selected. When this is the case, the Manual Weather State will be used instead. The Manual Weather State category below Basic Controls is the place where that manual state is controlled.\r\n\r\nYou can also use the Manual Weather State with the Change Weather function at [runtime_;runtime] if needed. Just call Change Weather without a preset selected for its input, and the weather will transition to the manual state instead.\r\n\r\nYou can also apply individual overrides to the local weather state, using the manual state values. For example, if weather is coming from the Thunderstorm preset, you could set Manual Rain Override to true, and set the Manual Rain value to have direct control of the rain value, while still having the rest of the state come from the Thunderstorm preset."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "2F979B8E4B463A5399312AA1978DE8D6", "Manual Weather State")` |
| `Keywords_8_5ACC585649ABDE1192D0EAB5258A2665` | `TArray` | `("manual weather state","manual weather","custom weather")` |
| `SubCategoryHeading_15_F6EBA06941D30788CC14989999E6C63B` | `bool` | `False` |

### Row `MaterialEffects`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `1` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "31045D304A33FB49FDCF6A9D631D6293", "Ultra Dynamic Weather can control [material_functions_;materialfunction] which make your materials respond to the weather\'s changing [material_state;materialstate] . Here are the material functions included:"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "DCFB53D54FCDAB76B58B9298EBCDCBE5", ">- Surface Weather Effects - For adding wetness, snow, and dust to solid surfaces. Intended for things like props and scenery objects, but not large ground/landscape materials. Can also render animated dripping and droplets effects on wet surfaces.\r\n\r\n- Dynamic Landscape Weather Effects - Can add both dynamic snow/dust coverage and wetness/puddles to ground materials, particularly landscape materials. The snow/dust and puddles can respond to interactions caused by a special component placed on moving objects.\r\n\r\n- Glass Window Rain Drips - Intended for use on flat transparent glass surfaces. Renders falling water droplets which form in rain.\r\n\r\n- Foliage Wind Movement - Outputs a world position offset which can deform a mesh using simple noise based animation, scaled by the current wind intensity. Intended for foliage models mainly.\r\n\r\n- Water Surface Rain Ripples - Adds animated raindrop impacts to the normal of a water surface."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "CD968C674E8C3FA407BC569E66677A49", "The behavior of the material state can be adjusted from the Material Effects category on UDW. A key setting here is \"Simulate Changing Material State Over Time\". If that\'s enabled, then at [runtime_;runtime] the material state will change over time based on the weather. For example, as it snows, material snow coverage will slowly increase. The time over which this happens for each type of weather can be found in the Material Effects category as well.\r\n\r\nIf you instead disable Simulate Changing Material State Over Time, then the material state at runtime will come directly from the current [weather_state;weatherstate] . So, for example, if you suddenly changed from Snow to Partly Cloudy, the material snow coverage would disappear instantly, because it\'s directly using the material snow coverage value from the Partly Cloudy weather state, which is 0."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "690012F7464827A211D91C9AE14E7136", "Material Effects Overview")` |
| `Keywords_8_5ACC585649ABDE1192D0EAB5258A2665` | `TArray` | `("snow","wet","material","materials","material effects","material functions","drips","dripping","surface","puddles","puddle")` |
| `SubCategoryHeading_15_F6EBA06941D30788CC14989999E6C63B` | `bool` | `False` |
| `SuggestedEntries_19_9776F58E45A513F145D90BBE28516AA1` | `TArray` | `("WeatherMaskBrushes","CustomMaterialEffects","What_Is_WeatherState")` |

### Row `Mobile`

| Field | Type | Value |

| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "606A59C34B272D9F15D3ADBF307F63AE", "If building for mobile devices, take note of a few settings in particular."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "3B7E84D2414C3D826387BF86683D9F0A", ">- Make certain you have changed the [Feature_Level_;featurelevel] setting in Basic Controls to match the feature level you are building for. For most mobile projects this will be the Mobile option. It\'s important this Feature Level setting is set properly so that the blueprint doesn\'t try to activate features which the device doesn\'t support, resulting in visual bugs or improper rendering.\r\n\r\n- In the mobile category, there are additional settings which define what Feature Level does when it is set to mobile.\r\n\r\n- In the mobile category, you can also find the Platform Feature Levels map, which can be used to determine feature level based on the platform name on startup."))` |
