### Row `SurfaceWeatherEffects`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `1` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "F31AC7B6409E22482088008E7E516AB8", "Surface Weather Effects is a [material_function_;materialfunction] which can make a solid surface appear wet and gather snow and dust coverage, as controlled by the current [material_state_;materialstate] on UDW. It can also apply optional effects for dripping and small droplets on wet surfaces.\r\n\r\nSurface Weather Effects is intended for props, architecture, and other solid scenery objects. It\'s not intended for expansive ground surfaces like landscapes. For that, I\'d suggest using the Dynamic Landscape Weather Effects.\r\n\r\nYou can see an example of a material using Surface Weather Effects in the [UDS_demo_map;demomap] ."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "326CB7574E06AFF7C08890B8843B787A", "^Setup"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "DEFDCFB442CA2CD5D3B0BA9E0C332786", ">To add Surface Weather Effects to a material, search the [material_palette_;materialpalette] for Weather and select Surface Weather Effects.\r\n\r\nYou should typically place the function right at the end of your material graph, before the material result.\r\n\r\nSurface Weather Effects uses a Material Attributes input and output. This is a pin which combines together all possible [material_attributes_;materialattributes] into one. If your material doesn\'t use one of these for its result, you can use Make Material Attributes and Break Material Attributes nodes to adjust for that.\r\n\r\nUse Static Bool nodes to provide True or False inputs for Apply Wetness and Apply Snow / Dust. This tells the function which effects you want to be applied to the surface. For example, if your project will only ever need wet materials but not snow or dust, you could plug True into Apply Wetness and False into Apply Snow / Dust, to save on material complexity.\r\n\r\nNote that by default the textures used for the effects will be mapped using world space coordinates. This is a good fit for static scenery/architecture. But if your material is going to be used on a moving object or a skeletal mesh, you should plug True into Local Space or For Skeletal Mesh, to configure the function for those cases."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "0902D85F4463FD344C67ECADEA6551C5", "^Dripping and Droplets"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "94F36AF14D4E9D1B0763B3998F60341B", ">To enable additional effects on wet surfaces, you can plug True into the Dripping and Droplets inputs.\r\n\r\nDripping enables an effect of rivulets of water moving down the surface where wet.\r\n\r\nDroplets enables an effect of very small water droplets which cling to a smooth surface.\r\n\r\nBoth of these effects are influenced by Porosity. This input generally represents how porous/permeable the surface is. 0 would be a surface like car paint or smooth plastic. 1 would be something like rough concrete or sand. Without an input, Porosity will be derived from the input roughness."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "52BF97B04280F29866415E8678AC7ECA", "^Snow/Dust Coverage on Rotating Models"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "6734B0AB4872EE723BE13DBBFFBE037B", ">If you use the snow/dust coverage on a moving model, with Local Space or For Skeletal Mesh enabled, you\'ll notice the direction of the snow/dust coverage rotates with the model. This is because the local normal is what is used for effects in local space.\r\n\r\nThere is a component you can add to an actor which can correct for this. It\'s \"Material Snow Dust Reorient\". Add it as a child of the mesh, and on begin play add a dynamic material instance for the surface using the weather effects to the \"Dynamic Material Instances\" array on the component.\r\n\r\nThe component will periodically monitor the rotation of the model and if needed, start slowly reorienting the direction of the snow/dust coverage to face global up. The settings for the speeds and update periods for this are exposed on the component."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "2AC5BF154964EF6C4A6898852E7839BF", "Surface Weather Effects")` |
| `Keywords_8_5ACC585649ABDE1192D0EAB5258A2665` | `TArray` | `("surface weather effects","snow coverage","dust coverage","wetness","material","material wetness","dripping","droplets")` |

### Row `T_UDS_Overview`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `2` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "46852AAD45F56094C7BA089ABCF96905", "Here is a brief look at UDS\' overall blueprint structure, to start off."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "CA5DA0434544B329448B88915DB08FEC", "^Startup"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "1882613448C6C6B7D6BF028ADEA5FDC2", "> The function Startup Sky is the one which contains all of UDS\' startup logic, shared when run from Construction Script in the editor, and on begin play when starting the level. It\'s also called to restart the sky at runtime, like when applying a configuration or changing sky mode during play.\r\n\r\nThe Startup Sky function handles all of the logic which only needs setting up once at startup, and it does the first run of the Update functions."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "6B08C86D42411B39771C23915F1291C6", "^Update Functions"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "B0065A9848018406AECA52B402E1957B", "> Update Static Variables and Update Active Variables are the two update functions, used to apply changes to properties on the components and material instances.\r\n\r\nUpdate Active Variables is for applying properties which change with time, weather, or other variables which are expected to commonly change at runtime. Update Active Variables is called frequently while the level is running, to update with these changes.\r\n\r\nUpdate Static Variables is for properties which aren\'t expected to change at runtime. It\'s run as part of construction script and once on event begin play, but won\'t run again at runtime unless called manually."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "BC399C95495F1944FE3412BCDAFECF31", "^Cache System"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "C55DC609483A06448BFFAFB977B69240", "> If Project Mode is set to Game/Real-Time, UDS utilizes a cache system which spreads out complex calculations so they don\'t have to happen every time Update Active Variables is run.\r\n\r\nThe function which caches these values is called Cache Properties. See the section below about the cache system for more information on how that works."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "DEFAC5E843072160C0B2CEAA192D0E02", "^General Organization"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "FE074D6A485BD221057C28BF0CCC4AFD", "> For finding functions relevant to any of the specific features on UDS, take note first that the functions are categorized generally by feature. For example, the function which applies static properties for the lens flare is called \"Static Properties - Lens Flare\" and is in the Lens Flare category.\r\n\r\nAlso note that nearly every function has a description which should give a general idea of what purpose it serves and how it\'s used."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "35C789824149283758027BB41B619F30", "Overview")` |
| `Keywords_8_5ACC585649ABDE1192D0EAB5258A2665` | `TArray` | — |

### Row `TD_UDS_CacheSystem`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `2` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "78C9963546BAEE3C32BCBA8B1217E136", "The cache system exists to spread out calculations of changing properties, so that they don\'t have to run every time Update Active Variables is called.\r\n\r\nThe function which does this is called Cache Properties. It uses a set of functions to cache values of different data types to arrays of new and old values. These cached values are then lerped from old to new between updates of the cache.\r\n\r\nThe update period of the cache is not constant. It changes to be more frequent when faster changes are called for. The function which handles that is called Monitor for Changes. It looks at how time and weather variables are changing on each frame and these change speeds are used to affect cache timing immediately if necessary. The cache timing itself is handled from the function Increment Cache Timer.\r\n\r\nNote, because Cache Properties operates essentially separately from the update functions, it has some of its own variables for things like Cached Sun Vector or Cached Moon Phase. Values which need to be shared by all of the cached properties, but aren\'t always the exact same as the actual current values for things like Sun Vector or Moon Phase.\r\n\r\nAs properties are cached by Cache Properties, the functions which apply the cached properties are bound to event dispatchers, which are called from Update Active Variables. These Apply functions all have the prefix AP, for Apply Properties."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "03B5AEB648B479DFB81C5F973960A67C", "Cache System")` |
| `Keywords_8_5ACC585649ABDE1192D0EAB5258A2665` | `TArray` | — |

### Row `TD_UDS_Clouds`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `2` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "B671694A4ECBACCDC8DD1780928894A5", "Most of the properties for the clouds are handled in the Update functions, but cloud movement in particular (for Volumetric Clouds and 2D Dynamic Clouds) is handled in its own functions, called Increment Cloud Movement Cache and Update Cloud Movement.\r\n\r\nIncrement Cloud Movement Cache is run a couple times a second by default, and it finds the current speed and direction that the cloud position should be offset, and caches the new position and old position.\r\n\r\nUpdate Cloud Movement runs on tick, and just takes those cached values and applies them to the material parameters for the visible clouds.\r\n\r\nNote that the properties used for the volumetric clouds, both here and in the Update functions, are being set on a shared material parameter collection called UDS_VolumetricClouds_MPC. This is used to allow many different materials for things like cloud fog and cloud shadows to approximate cloud coverage using the same properties sampled by the visible clouds."))` |

### Row `TD_UDS_Replication`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `2` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "5246CC0E43F5FA11C9217DB38F83338E", "Time of Day and Date will be replicated in a multiplayer environment. (For info about weather state replication, see the UDW replication section below.)\r\n\r\nTime of Day\'s replication works by only periodically updating the \"Replicated Time of Day\" variable, which notifies clients to update Time of Day using the replicated value. Properties which directly inform how fast time moves forward (Day Length, Night Length, Time Speed, Simulation Speed) are replicated themselves. This way the client can handle moving time forward locally most of the time, the same as its handled by the server. Then it resyncs when Replicated Time of Day is updated."))` |

### Row `TD_UDS_TimeandLighting`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `2` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "20592D19444A87A23EA495801908B576", "Time is handled through manipulation of Time of Day and the Date variables. The sun and moon rotations are derived from time (unless Manual Position options are in use) and the rotations of the sun and moon are used by Cache Properties and Update Active Variables to influence properties like fog color or light intensities.\r\n\r\nTime of Day is manipulated on tick through the functions Time of Day Animation and Apply System Time, if either of those features is active.\r\n\r\nDate is only manipulated by UDS at midnight, to increment the day forward using the function Offset Date.\r\n\r\nSun and Moon rotation are cached values, so their rotation is determined in the function Cache Sun and Moon Orientation. The logic used in that function will depend on if the Simulate option is true for either the sun or moon. If it is, then the function Approximate Real Sun Moon and Stars is what handles the simulated rotations based on the time, date and coordinates.\r\n\r\nNote, this cached orientation is only applied constantly to the Sun World Rotation and Moon World Rotation variables which hold the rotation to be used for the visuals. The lights themselves have settings (the Lights Update settings in the Directional Light category) which allow the lights to only periodically change rotation, so the rotation variables act as an intermediary.\r\n\r\nUpdate Active Variables will then use the forward vector of the Sun World Rotation and Moon World Rotation to determine many properties which change with the lights orientation."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "765E5EE94A95C1A19A9EDBA3AE5F58EF", "Time and Lighting")` |

| Field | Type | Value |

The manager class is found in Blueprints/Weather_Effects/System.\r\n\r\nIf the simulate option is disabled, the material state will always come directly from the weather state objects informing the global state."))` |

### Row `TD_UDW_NiagaraSystems`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `2` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "649F711442351FB8573D3388BA9EB23A", "The niagara systems used by UDW can be found in the Particles folder."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "1C22252147012C040FD666817F3500CD", "^Weather Particles"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "B03C9D03476FD0FB0662BCAB15A27092", "> The Rain, Dust, Snow, and Wind Debris system assets can be found in the Particles folder.\r\n\r\nThese systems share many modules and parent emitters, since much of their behavior is the same.\r\n\r\nThey all use a CPU Collision and GPU Collision emitter, which handle filling the niagara arrays with valid particle paths. UDW toggles one of these emitters off when it constructs the system, depending the selected setting for Particle Collision Mode.\r\n\r\nThe rest of the emitters sample the arrays randomly to get a valid particle path, to control their location, velocity, and lifetime."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "310F20AB48DC9824D6556CB672E37374", "^Lightning"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "8948A4324AD0CBA2EF5D608170DE5CE0", ">The Lightning Strike niagara system is the one used for lightning flashes with a visible lightning bolt. The Obscured Lightning system is used for the passive effect of flashes which just light the clouds."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "F1715CDA4CA1410E673FA198BFBF29AF", "On UDW, the niagara components for the weather particles and obscured lightning are controlled mainly from the update functions. The lightning flashes are spawned from the Lightning Flash graph."))` |

### Row `TD_UDW_Overview`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `2` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "D531752E4818CD37ED2E789B5D02F203", "The blueprint structure of UDW is modeled after UDS."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "44E2EEC24239B6E2F809D0A143B2DA88", "^Startup"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "047EDE9140F0EAF0410BDA88C84BB31F", ">UDW has a function similar to Startup Sky on UDS. On UDW it\'s called Start Weather System.\r\n\r\nThis handles creating the necessary objects, like weather settings objects, and starting systems like random weather variation. It also does the first run of the update functions."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "659E1E1B44E6B2E3CC56E7A18B7A8687", "^Update Current Global and Local Weather State"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "10155B934E83E565F10F2BA156CB92A2", ">This function is what creates the composite global state and local state, if needed, during tick."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "F426190746883A8E144C1E8CC1152511", "^Monitor Local Weather Changes"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "8D14A799482DC153DACCB4BC32EE803E", "> This function runs after the local weather state is generated, looking for any values which have changed past a threshold. Any that have changed get a set of relevant functions bound to a dispatcher called in Update Active Variables, to apply changes to anything which responds to that state value."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "0E892CAC490C8BFFA60767AC1FF79BDB", "^Update Functions"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "D0B1C9884F77B2DD2B5E0FADF1CFF926", ">Update Active Variables and Update Static Variables exist in much the same way as they do on UDS.\r\n\r\nUpdate Active Variables handles applying changes to niagara systems, sound components, and material effects, which change with the weather.\r\n\r\nUpdate Static Variables applies properties which aren\'t expected to change with the weather, like the max spawn distance of the weather particles for example."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "70FBA0D64F6013F701C5E9961337D112", "^General Organization"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "5D52CEC146B23904FAEEE3A0BB0BDE50", ">Just like on UDS, the functions on UDW are categorized generally based on the feature they relate to. Each function also has a description, explaining what it\'s for and where it\'s used."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "E02271AD4EA1AC10C44721B4CE63D407", "Overview")` |

### Row `TD_UDW_Replication`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `2` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "FA978EF5469CA5AD9678669D6F83DD4A", "Weather state is replicated by UDW for multiplayer. Specifically, the Global Weather State on UDW is replicated, as well as the state on Weather Override Volumes and the state of Radial Storms. The clients then determine their Local Weather State themselves, so each player can experience their own local weather, but the states inside and outside of volumes/storms will be shared.\r\n\r\nThe global state isn\'t replicated directly, but by replicating the weather preset assets used by the transition system, the random weather variation, and the weather override volumes. This way the client can only receive updates when a change of state on one of those sources starts, and handle global weather state reliably in the same way as the server between those updates."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "ADCDD8BE4B8F8BD85E64D0A2A2A578E9", "Replication")` |
| `Keywords_8_5ACC585649ABDE1192D0EAB5258A2665` | `TArray` | — |

### Row `TD_UDW_Sound`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `2` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "37B54CF440C703C6A30C58B25C9D8298", "Much of the sound effects logic exists in the MetaSound assets. These are found in Sound/MetaSounds.\r\n\r\nUDW just updates the audio components periodically with the relevant weather state values, sound occlusion values, and volume levels. The values are interpolated using the update period, in the MetaSound graphs.\r\n\r\nThe sounds for weather are handled by two sources, Global and Directional. Global sounds are not panned/spatialized, and Directional sounds are. Directional sounds also have their sound occlusion applied directionally, so if the X+ direction is blocked, directional sounds in that direction will be attenuated.\r\n\r\nThe Global and Directional sources both output to an audio bus called UDS_Weather_AudioBus. This bus is used by another source on UDW called the Sound Mixer, which applies the necessary stereo panning and sound occlusion to all the weather sounds together, and outputs that to the base submix.\r\n\r\nThe occlusion values used for sound are calculated by the Player Occlusion component on UDS."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "0D8EB50E41B326E7818A52946C8F6871", "Sound")` |
| `Keywords_8_5ACC585649ABDE1192D0EAB5258A2665` | `TArray` | — |

### Row `TD_UDW_WeatherState`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `2` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "3C26CBE54C846C74A12F9F923172FB16", "The weather state on UDW is determined in two stages, the Global Weather State and the Local Weather State."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "A6EF3D994FF2BD91BE82F88DC90DD9D0", "^Global Weather State"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "2A2EF43F44C36CC04DD09793737BECC8", "> The global weather state is the state determined by the weather settings on UDW itself. This would be the weather settings preset, the Change Weather function, and the random weather variation.\r\n\r\nBind Global State Update Functions is called when anything which influences global state changes, for example a weather transition starting.\r\n\r\nThat function binds the global state update functions needed to a dispatcher called Construct Global Weather. That dispatcher is called in the function Update Current Global and Local Weather State.\r\n\r\nThe functions which can be bound do things like applying the weather preset, handling transitions if active, applying the random weather state, and incrementing the global material state sim."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "4C323C4A47432CB7B8DBA8A7E4625664", "^Local Weather State"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "2EEE94074020FB371C95FABDD44BEAD2", ">The construction of the local weather state is handled in much the same way. The binding function is called as needed to bind functions to the Construct Local Weather dispatcher, which is called from Update Current Global and Local Weather State.\r\n\r\nThe Local Weather bindings handle things like applying weather override volumes, radial storms, and changes above the cloud layer."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "7DF42FB94AD5B16E7BD8C9BC0E0D5283", "In the Update Active Variables function, almost all of the properties set there will be sampling the values on the Local Weather State object, since that represents the weather state at the player\'s location."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "24CB23484219604D4AC93DAC51BEF2CC", "Weather State")` |

### Row `UDS_Modifiers`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `0` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "49BE01B3467BDEFC2CDFAA807C21F8B6", "UDS has a framework for applying modifiers to the sky, which can affect a selection of float and color properties on UDS, as well as post process settings. These modifiers can be applied or removed at [runtime,_;runtime] faded in and out, and layered on top of each other."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "DC3877CC4D962230B0DF2EBD5AF7D865", "***"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "CF70321149A08BA0FE951BB0FC8EAE1C", "^Creating Sky Modifier Assets"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "1F6B74F949CE01F2906A0FB26BB137D3", ">UDS Modifiers are data assets which you can author using the Sky Modifier Editor utility. You can access this from the Ultra Dynamic Sky dropdown on the level editor toolbar, or by running the editor utility asset in Blueprints/Tools.\r\n\r\nIn the Sky Modifier Editor, you can Open an existing UDS Modifier asset, or use New to create a new blank modifier. New modifier assets are placed in Blueprints/Sky_Modifiers, but after they\'re saved by the tool, you are free to move them anywhere else.\r\n\r\nThe Modifiable Sky Properties lists all the properties which the modifier system can take control of on UDS. To make the current modifier affect one of these, just edit the value exposed for it. If you want to remove that property override, click the checkbox next to the property to remove it from the modifier.\r\n\r\nIn Modifier Settings, you can also adjust the easing behavior used when fading the modifier in/out, as well as the max alpha this modifier will apply when interpolating to its override values. This is also where you can enable the option for the modifier to apply its own post process settings, and configure the settings it applies.\r\n\r\nWhile you work in the Sky Modifier Editor, the current modifier will be previewed on UDS."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "C6D5A45E413B033446CED5B7BB2EAD2E", "***"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "24EF08D6422106C8268BDA9F7AC39530", "You can add a modifier to the sky configuration, to be used from level start, from the Modifiers category on UDS. You can also toggle the visibility of that modifier in the level editor.\r\n\r\nAt runtime, there are functions you can call on UDS to control modifiers:"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "D71992B94C010333AFC16789D06EF206", "^Add Modifier"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "47439D9E4308ECDF13CD23984AA9471F", ">This function will add a modifier if it is not already present, and fade it in over the supplied fade in time, in seconds."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "9C03959A48ABB47D539F4EA0BF3DE753", "^ Remove Modifier"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "C9A565174FB604AA198C1A868956BE73", ">Similarly, this function will remove an existing applied modifier, and fade it out over the supplied fade out time."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "9CE67FB4473C8B4EB76104ACAE1C4DAF", "^Set Modifier State"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "7B10B84C428D10F778E5F9AD4C7A2A16", ">This function will set the alpha of a modifier in a way that it will not change on its own. For example, you could use this function to manually make a modifier be controlled by an arbitrarily changing value, like the player\'s position in the level. Note, the modifier does not need to already be applied to call this function. If it\'s not, this function will add it automatically."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "980ED2964686360CC63AE493324BACAC", "^Clear Modifiers"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "53D7271D423AAC1470E31FA6DB9D0CAE", ">Instantly clears out all applied modifiers at once."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "5410DE6042E255D9609BC987E2D763D3", "^Set Unmodified Property Values"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "C1FC857247E2E095719A678DF26CAEA4", ">The blueprint, when it starts up, saves all of its unmodified properties, for the modifiers to interpolate from/to as they are added and removed. If you need to, you can call this function again at runtime to resave the current applied properties to be the new unmodified state."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "9E6ED0AC42D22069161934A001F84B87", "***"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "57BFDC414F4D130026D67EAFC58DAEFE", "^Time of Day Specific Modifiers"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "2831768B42B398BEC28CD6B788289366", ">If you want a modifier to apply on its own within a specific Time of Day range, there is a feature for that as well. In the Sky Modifiers category, find the map called Time of Day Specific Modifiers.\r\n\r\nAdd a modifier to that map, and expand the dropdown to open the settings for its fade range. You can configure the modifier to fade in across any range of Time of Day values and fade out across another. You can have the fade in happen before or after the fade out, for cases where the modifier is applied overnight. Just make sure the end time for both fades is after the start time.\r\n\r\nWhen applying a modifier automatically with time in this way, do not attempt to control it with the modifier control functions mentioned above, as they will conflict."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "7BA0082A42CF289DB9FA2482ABEC61FF", "Sky Modifiers")` |

### Row `UpdatingUDS`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `0` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "DEE991A54667D9D8D54D7AAA705E08F1", "You can check if there are updates available for UDS by going to the update history document, linked on the home page of this documentation utility.\r\n\r\nUDS updates can be installed to your project without you losing your work with the assets. Still, I would recommend backing up or using version control before updating, so you can always roll back if anything does go wrong with an update process.\r\n\r\nUnderstand, updating the UDS assets means overwriting them with the new versions. So any modifications you\'ve made directly to the assets (like opening UDS in the blueprint editor and changing its blueprint logic for example) will be lost. Additional files you\'ve created within the UDS folder, like Configuration assets or Sky Modifiers, will remain, since they won\'t be overwritten by anything.\r\n\r\nNote, the Fab plugin cannot be used to update an asset pack already in your project. To update, you will need to use the Epic launcher.\r\n\r\nHow you update will depend on if UDS is still in its default location (Content/UltraDynamicSky)."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "70263E554E323667E8EB49B93427234C", "^If UDS is in its default location:"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "AB12277C4117A65B76497C8EF2278948", ">With UDS where the launcher expects it to be, you can do the update in one simple step.\r\n\r\nMake sure your project is not open before updating.\r\n\r\nIn the launcher, find Ultra Dynamic Sky in the Fab library section, under the Library tab.\r\n\r\nSelect Add to Project on UDS and when it prompts you to overwrite the old files, allow it to do so.\r\n\r\nIf the launcher has any problem with adding or doesn\'t download the latest version, try selecting Remove Local Content on UDS and trying again. This will usually fix launcher issues like that."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "FDBDAE8F4C2E3E99E99B619AF9DC27ED", "^If you have moved UDS to a different location in your project:"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "AEE13A57446B65922EF0598F7307D552", ">With UDS not in its default location, the process is more involved. You will have to perform the same move in another project and then copy it over manually, as the editor will have to adjust all the asset references within the folder to match where it is in the target project.\r\n\r\nFirst, in your target project, run Update Redirector References on the UltraDynamicSky folder to ensure it isn\'t relying on redirectors. Close your target project.\r\n\r\nFrom the launcher, add UDS to a blank project in the same engine version as your target project.\r\n\r\nOpen the blank project, and open the UDS demo map. Let it finish compiling shaders if it needs to.  With the demo map still open, move the UltraDynamicSky folder to a directory which exactly matches where it is in the target project. Wait for the editor to finish the move, and then right click the entire Content folder and select Update Redirector References.\r\n\r\nClose and open the UDS demo map to confirm the editor hasn\'t broken anything when moving files. If some things aren\'t visible like clouds, you may need to use the console command \"Recompileshaders All\" to fix for an engine bug with shader compilation after assets are moved.\r\n\r\nClose the project, and make sure the target project isn\'t open either. From a file explorer, copy and paste the UltraDynamicSky folder from the blank project over to your target project, overwriting the old UltraDynamicSky folder.\r\n\r\nOpen the target project and the update should be applied cleanly."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "FA5B616449182046FFC3D0AF3B116BA7", "***"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "46B2D31A4800D15453CA95A2434D8FFE", "^After Installing an Update"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "850E0A7A44560EC293698FBF991656AD", "With an update to UDS successfully installed, I would recommend reading the full change logs for any updates you got. You can find these in the Update History document linked on the home page of this utility. The change log will be the place where you\'ll find any info about work you may need to do in your project to support the new version."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "BA5F81524781D25CD704939933A429E2", "How to Update UDS")` |
| `Keywords_8_5ACC585649ABDE1192D0EAB5258A2665` | `TArray` | `("update","install update","patch","hotfix","version","upgrade")` |

### Row `VolCloudLightRays`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `0` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "2A4A91EA4B82B762E26D84B73E217D93", "If in an overcast sky you use the [Volumetric_Cloud_Painter_;volcloudpainter] to create a break in the cloud coverage, you will see an effect of light rays in the distance coming down through that hole in the coverage. That\'s a result of the Volumetric Cloud Light Rays, which are enabled by default, and can be adjusted in the category of the same name.\r\n\r\nNote, the volumetric cloud light rays are a custom effect which renders rays using giant additive cards controlled by a niagara system. They aren\'t connected in any way to volumetric fog or screen space light shafts.\r\n\r\nThere are settings in the Volumetric Cloud Light Rays category to adjust the color and spacing of the ray cards, as well as enable \"Individual Cloud Light Rays\" which will try to cast rays through gaps in overall high coverage cloud formations, not just painted gaps in coverage. Note that this setting can potentially render many more ray cards, so it can have a more significant performance cost."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "7BCFDF3D4F4ED05D270524A4CF22FC79", "Volumetric Cloud Light Rays")` |
| `Keywords_8_5ACC585649ABDE1192D0EAB5258A2665` | `TArray` | `("volumetric cloud light rays","light rays","cloud light rays")` |
| `SubCategoryHeading_15_F6EBA06941D30788CC14989999E6C63B` | `bool` | `False` |
| `SuggestedEntries_19_9776F58E45A513F145D90BBE28516AA1` | `TArray` | `("VolClouds","Paint_Volumetric_Clouds")` |

### Row `VolClouds`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `0` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "FF7D3859439EA2A5F200C1B1F2B5A54C", "The Volumetric Clouds category is where you\'ll find the settings for adjusting the appearance of the [volumetric_cloud_;volumetricclouds] layer. Here are some of the key settings and what they do:"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "70E698AA44C5F53F958114B202FBE541", ">- [Volumetric_Cloud_Rendering_Mode_;volcloudrendermode] is what determines how the engine will render the volumetric clouds to the screen. (It\'s a control for the renderer cvar r.volumetricrendertarget.mode, exposed through the UDS details for convenience) The modes are named after what aspects of rendering they prioritize. This setting has performance implications, and each mode has different strengths and weaknesses. See the tooltips for the modes for an explanation of each.\r\n\r\n- Bottom Altitude is what sets how high the cloud layer is in the level. It\'s recommended to use this option instead of moving the UDS actor, as Bottom Altitude will adjust only the cloud layer, and won\'t have unintended effects on atmosphere and fog.\r\n\r\n- Volumetric Clouds Scale is what you should adjust if you want to scale the entire cloud field uniformly.\r\n\r\n- The View Sample Scale settings are what control the amount of samples used to render the clouds. If they\'re looking too noisy, you can increase this setting to resolve the clouds better, at a performance cost.\r\n\r\n- In the Second Cloud Layer dropdown, Two Layers can be enabled to add a second layer of clouds above the first, offset in a handful of ways using the Layer 2 settings. Note that a second layer will increase the cost of cloud rendering very significantly."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "66D7D68D485F2CDAE4ECCDA1A60066F1", "If you want to directly control volumetric cloud coverage in specific parts of your level, like to make a specific area around a mountain free of clouds for example, you should use the [Volumetric_Cloud_Painter_;volcloudpainter] utility. There is a section specifically on the Volumetric Cloud Painter further down in this document.\r\n\r\nFor more advanced control over cloud shaping, a tool is included for authoring the Cloud Profile LUT texture UDS clouds sample for their shape. That tool is the Cloud Profile Authoring Tool. You can run it from the Ultra Dynamic Sky dropdown on the level editor toolbar, or run the editor utility found in Blueprints/Tools."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "F3EA3BE440ABE596CBE13F9FF7225C83", "Volumetric Clouds")` |
| `Keywords_8_5ACC585649ABDE1192D0EAB5258A2665` | `TArray` | `("clouds","appearance","volumetric clouds","volumetric","altitude")` |
| `SubCategoryHeading_15_F6EBA06941D30788CC14989999E6C63B` | `bool` | `False` |
| `SuggestedEntries_19_9776F58E45A513F145D90BBE28516AA1` | `TArray` | `("Paint_Volumetric_Clouds","CloudShadows")` |

### Row `VolumetricFog`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `0` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "EC363E914CBD4C315A3D7FAE7AA7E19D", "Volumetric Fog is a rendering feature in Unreal Engine which can render more advanced fog nearby the camera, which receives and scatters light from local light sources and can vary its color and extinction using volumetric materials or particles placed in the level.\r\n\r\nThe settings for enabling this on UDS are found in its Volumetric Fog category.\r\n\r\nThe basic settings for enabling volumetric fog and adjusting its overall extinction and the distance it renders from the camera are found at the top of the category. You\'ll also find settings for the sun and moon\'s Volumetric Scattering Intensity here, which scales how much each light source lights up the volumetric fog."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "76D67A2E42B46BE835A9C5BB865FDA19", "***"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "A56042C9480968F7584100947069B855", "^Global Volumetric Material"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "C70D362C4D1BCC99344E08B26BD85547", "Also in the Volumetric Fog category is the option to render the Global Volumetric Material, which if enabled will allow some simple global controls of extinction and color. The global volumetric material has the following features, each of which can be enabled/adjusted from here in the Volumetric Fog category:"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "B54091AE4326CF25FF50159B8EC6492B", ">- Texture based 3D noise applied to the fog extinction, to add some variation to the fog.\r\n\r\n- The ability to mask the volumetric fog using the Weather Mask brush system. See the weather section of this readme for information about that toolset.\r\n\r\n- Ground fog, which adds additional fog extinction in the air directly above distance fields. This requires the project setting to generate mesh distance fields to be enabled.\r\n\r\n- Specific fog extinction and albedo can be applied beneath the water level. The water level is controlled from the Water category."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "07D6D2CF4E98BDC5752F6293260E080D", "Volumetric Fog")` |
| `Keywords_8_5ACC585649ABDE1192D0EAB5258A2665` | `TArray` | `("volumetric","fog","volumetric fog","mist","foggy")` |
| `SubCategoryHeading_15_F6EBA06941D30788CC14989999E6C63B` | `bool` | `False` |
| `SuggestedEntries_19_9776F58E45A513F145D90BBE28516AA1` | `TArray` | `("FogDensity","WeatherMaskBrushes")` |

### Row `WaterLevelUDW`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `1` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "636925D54FB1DC803C7C7CAB065D8108", "If you have a global water height in your level, like for an ocean, there are features on UDW to make the weather effects be universally affected by that water level.\r\n\r\nThe option for this is found in the Water Level category. Just enable Use UDS Water Level and set the water level in Ultra Dynamic Sky\'s Water category.\r\n\r\nHere is all the water level can affect:"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "73A4AF6048B31FDBB3CE089200EF87C1", ">- Weather particles will be kept from traveling or spawning beneath the water level.\r\n\r\n- Sound Occlusion will be fully occluded when the player camera goes below the water level.\r\n\r\n- Screen Droplets will turn off automatically when the camera goes underwater and the screen will be wet when the camera comes back out of the water.\r\n\r\n- The Rainbow will be masked beneath the water level if the option for it is enabled.\r\n\r\n- The Surface Weather Effects and Dynamic Landscape Weather Effects functions have inputs to enable masking of coverage below the water level."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "2AFFFE5146B9DBD781D902AA484CE8DD", "Water Level")` |
| `Keywords_8_5ACC585649ABDE1192D0EAB5258A2665` | `TArray` | `("water","ocean","water level","water height","underwater")` |
| `SubCategoryHeading_15_F6EBA06941D30788CC14989999E6C63B` | `bool` | `False` |
| `SuggestedEntries_19_9776F58E45A513F145D90BBE28516AA1` | `TArray` | `("SoundOcclusion","Rainbow","ScreenDroplets","Caustics")` |

### Row `WaterSurfaceRainRipples`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `1` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "015C0F81422B10330BB3E8AC51C4EC1F", "Water Surface Rain Ripples is a [material_function_;materialfunction] which adds ripples to the normal of a water surface, based on the amount of rain on UDW."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "35B7B9C54E1B741F3ACBADA74AD6E007", "^Setup"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "97CCFE734F5FEB06C1DA759F7FF43B97", ">To add Water Surface Rain Ripples to your material, search the [material_palette_;materialpalette] for Weather and select Water Surface Rain Ripples.\r\n\r\nTypically you should put the function at the very end of the material graph, right before the material result. This function just modifies the normal [attribute;materialattributes] , so you should only need to give it your material\'s normal as an input and plug its normal output into the material result.\r\n\r\nThe two additional inputs can be used to scale the ripple effect texture, and adjust how intense it is in affecting the normal."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "F8DE607B46C8E1F86093D29A10050188", "Water Surface Rain Ripples")` |

| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `1` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "EA4ED8954F3D67C82DBCA598F526890F", "The Weather Settings Presets are the preconfigured weather states like Thunderstorm, Partly Cloudy, and Blizzard. They\'re used for the Weather variable in Basic Controls, as well as by the [Change_Weather_;changeweather] function, [Random_Weather_Variation;randomweathervariation] , [Weather_Override_Volumes;weatheroverridevolume] , and [Radial_Storms.;radialstorm]\r\n\r\nYou can find the included presets in Blueprints/Weather_Effects/Weather_Presets."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "93F75C504E4EC5BE2A50439FF09681FB", "[IMAGE]\r\nhttps://imagedelivery.net/dJ8zT5MNjUXoua7duc582w/b0faba35-1376-4650-6a95-4c8612828600/public\r\nThe data assets for the weather settings presets, in their folder."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "ADF0F5984AE9BA93884144A02E93FDF9", "To make your own, a good way is to just duplicate one of the assets in that folder and adjust the settings in the new preset. Your new asset will be usable in all the same ways that the included presets are.\r\n\r\nIt\'s also possible to add additional blueprint logic into individual weather presets for custom effects. See the entry on Custom Weather Behavior for that."))` |

### Row `WeatherEventDIspatchers`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `1` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "F168FE444539C088BDDC669959F7F82F", "UDW has [event_dispatchers_;eventdispatcher] which your classes can bind to trigger events based on changes to the [weather_state.;weatherstate]"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "477F62C740B26EC45EAD069533DED885", ">- Started Raining and Finished Raining, triggered based on the amount of rain in the weather state.\r\n\r\n- Started Snowing and Finished Snowing, which is the same thing for snow.\r\n\r\n- Dust/Sand Forming and Dust/Sand clearing, which is the same for dust.\r\n\r\n- Getting Cloudy and Clouds Clearing, which is based on the cloud coverage in the weather state.\r\n\r\n- Getting Foggy and Fog Clearing, based on the Fog value in the weather state.\r\n\r\n- Weather Display Name Changed, which fires when the output of Get Display Name for Current Weather Changes. This is a good dispatcher to use to trigger something based on general weather changes."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "3D96869744DDB1A01C75F7856A6E837C", "For the started/finished events, you can adjust the threshold which triggers them from the Event Dispatchers category on UDW.\r\n\r\nThere are also dispatchers called State Change, which can be used to monitor specific weather state values for when they change. For example, you could bind to \"State Change - Rain\" to run logic whenever the amount of rain changes on UDW."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "D6F750EF4B6A36D615AC2B8E58CF5CA0", "Weather Event Dispatchers")` |

| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "F4B4A2C5467A4DD6D86AD797FD2B174D", "Ultra Dynamic Weather can add rain, snow, dust, lightning, material effects and more to your scene. You can control the weather state in several different ways from random variation to directly calling a weather change.\r\n\r\nThis section of the readme will walk through setting up UDW in your level, controlling the weather state in various ways, adding material functions to your project\'s materials for dynamic weather effects, and more."))` |

### Row `WeatherMaskBrushes`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `1` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "41A37FB14691913B9928358B62ACAFFC", "By default, the material effects for snow, dust and wetness will affect everywhere globally, across the whole scene. To mask the effects in specific spaces, they also sample from a [weather_mask_;weathermask] render target, which is drawn using components of two classes.\r\n\r\nYou can either use the component classes (found in Blueprints/Weather_Effects/Components) directly in your own actor classes, or you can use the included actor classes which contain one of these components (found in Blueprints/Weather_Effects). "),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "80818BA6459B0857A1B6D2BB6431285F", "***"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "9EDFA0FE4483C4E1730AA98571EE5DD0", "^Weather Mask Brush"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "D882A46D45B9F54D43E2248830D12BF5", "> The [Weather_Mask_Brush_;weathermaskbrush] will draw a simple shape or a painted texture, selectable using the variable \"Brush\". The brush actor can also be scaled non-uniformly and rotated on the Z axis. Because the system works by drawing these shapes into a render target, the shapes are always projected straight up and down on the Z axis.\r\n\r\nYou can adjust how much each brush affects snow or wetness with the variables \"Mask Wetness\" and \"Mask Snow/Dust\". There is also an option, called \"Cancel Masks Above\". This affects the entire rectangle the brush occupies, disabling any brush masking above the height of the actor.\r\n\r\nIf you need more control over the brush shape, you can paint a texture which the mask brush will use instead of the simple brush shapes. To do this, open the editor utility called Weather Mask Brush Painter. You can find it in the Ultra Dynamic Sky dropdown on the level editor toolbar, or in the Blueprints/Tools folder. With the painter open, select a weather mask brush actor and click the button to start painting.\r\n\r\nRight click to pan the painting area. Drag middle mouse to zoom. Click and drag with the left mouse to paint. See the settings on the top bar to adjust the painting brush and the value being painted.\r\n\r\nWhen finished, make sure to click Save, for the painted mask to be saved to a texture asset. This asset will be put in a folder called UDS_LevelData, in the folder where the level is saved."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "E1BD75014AB8F8C47FB1F3BF7DE03205", "***"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "A169781F40CC02A6E9639A8C63B8E655", "^Weather Mask Projection Box"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "D06F385147272829378208BA5A318C89", "> The [Weather_Mask_Projection_Box_;projectionbox] captures the meshes within the box, and uses those shapes to mask weather effects straight down. You can place a projection box around a complex structure like a building, and the shapes of the structure will occlude directly below.\r\n\r\nTry to place the box so it encompasses only the region of mesh geometry which needs to occlude downward. For example, you might place the box so it only contains the roof of a house. Also try to make sure the width and length of the box is as small as it can be to fit the occluding objects inside, to eliminate wasted space and resolution of the resulting render target.\r\n\r\nIn the exposed settings for the projection box, you can adjust the amount snow/dust and wetness are masked, as well as how much the mask beneath the box is blurred when drawn into the mask target."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "873A28584038EFA67E7E96A9BE8B39B1", "[IMAGE]\r\nhttps://imagedelivery.net/dJ8zT5MNjUXoua7duc582w/6bcd7f72-30ae-4bec-a915-d083c9aa2a00/public\r\nThe basic principle of positioning a projection box. It should enclose the parts of the mesh which need to project a mask downward."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "85ED35924EEA876326828996EE1384F2", "***"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "B289AC3E49D7D8B32E141EBCCDEFE496", "If you want any individual material or instance to ignore the weather mask actors, you can use the static switch parameters \"Apply Weather Mask Brushes to Wetness\" and \"Apply Weather Mask Brushes to Snow\" to disable the effects at the material level.\r\n\r\nThe effects of the mask will stop once they reach a certain distance from the camera. This is determined by the width of the render target they draw to for the masking. You can adjust that scale in the Weather Mask Target category on UDW.\r\n\r\nIf you need to fade the effect of a mask component over time, there is a function for this. On the Weather Mask Brush component or Weather Mask Projection Box component, call the function \"Fade Mask Over Time\". The fade will happen at 20 updates per second by default. This is determined by the setting Weather Mask Update Period on UDW."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "1F6EA8904383FAE8BF4BE0B0B1E62A0C", "Masking Material Effect Coverage")` |
| `Keywords_8_5ACC585649ABDE1192D0EAB5258A2665` | `TArray` | `("weather","mask","brush","weather mask brush","material effect","material effects","snow","puddles","weather mask tools")` |

### Row `WeatherOcclusionVolume`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `1` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "D0347ABE4EDFF355435D4CBB9BD6E4B4", "The Weather Occlusion Volume is a volume texture which contains a low resolution cache of the area around the camera position, and how occluded each point is from the weather/wind. It does this by sampling the global distance field, so it requires distance fields to be enabled and supported.\r\n\r\nThe Post Process Wind Fog can use this volume texture to mask its intensity in spaces blocked by scenery."))` |

### Row `WeatherOverrideVolumes`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `1` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "8F8CE2CF4C632E5634E776A3DC5D54E0", "For large maps, it may be necessary to change [weather_state_;weatherstate] by region. You can do this by using a [Weather_Override_Volume;weatheroverridevolume] , an actor found in the Weather Effects folder in Blueprints.\r\n\r\nTo adjust the area affected by the volume, edit the points of the spline component. You can right click on a point on the spline to add new spline points. You can also scale the actor, but try to avoid non-uniform scaling.\r\n\r\nConfiguring weather on a WOV is designed to be similar in structure to how UDW\'s global weather state is controlled. You can select a weather preset for the WOV to use in its Basic Controls category, and you can enable Random Weather Variation as well, with unique probability maps. Note the specifics of Random Weather Variation timing/logic will come from the settings on UDW, in its Random Weather Variation category.\r\n\r\nHere are some of the key settings on the Weather Override Volume:"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "F38A1F2C486AF7D5A8841A96BD2808C4", ">- Transition Width controls how much space is devoted to transitioning from the outside weather state to the inside weather state. The transition is completely spatial, so ideally the transition width should be very high, to offer a smooth transition between states as the player crosses into the region. The default transition width is small to keep the initial size of the actor reasonable as a starting point. An ideal WOV would typically be much larger, with a larger transition width to match.\r\n\r\n- Priority will determine the behavior when multiple volume actors overlap each other.\r\n\r\n- The Temperature category contains the temperature ranges used by UDW when the player is inside the region.\r\n\r\n- You can also apply a [climate_preset;climatepreset] , and it will work the same as applying one to UDS, changing the probability maps and the WOV\'s temperature ranges."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "1C3D754B43EDC6812693239A562137A5", "The location used to query the WOV for its affect on weather is determined by the Control Point Location Source, in Basic Controls on UDW.\r\n\r\nThe Weather Override Volumes will, by default, draw their [material_state_;materialstate] into a render target sampled by the weather material functions, so that for example a snowy region can appear snowy from outside, and from inside you can see the lack of snow coverage outside the region. This behavior can be disabled or adjusted on UDW, from the Weather Override Volumes category there.\r\n\r\nWeather Override Volumes also have functions which can be called to change their state at runtime, similar to UDW. There is a Change Weather function, which will transition to a specific static weather preset. And there is Change to Random Weather Variation, which will transition over to random weather.\r\n\r\nIf you want to use a Weather Override Volume to change anything other than the weather state on UDW, that is possible. To do this, create a child of the Weather Override Volume class, and on that child override the function called \"Custom Volume Behavior\". This function is run from UDW when it uses the WOV to affect local weather. The Alpha input represents how much the player is inside the volume, from 0 to 1."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "D051270748998EB5A2FF65BDEB0F2A1F", "Weather Override Volumes")` |
| `Keywords_8_5ACC585649ABDE1192D0EAB5258A2665` | `TArray` | `("weather","region","regional","location","position","positional","player","zone","weather zone","weather region","storm","biome","biomes","weather override volume")` |

### Row `WeatherParticleCollision`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `1` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "2417D8D246D9A902A44467AFC0853B8B", "The weather particles on UDW (rain, snow, dust) have a system of particle collision, so they can hit surfaces and stay out of interior spaces. This collision is enabled by default.\r\n\r\nCollision is selected with the option Particle Collision Mode. There are three modes: Simple Collision, Distance Field Collision, and No Collision."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "1B81A7A246D38FD0E858AB8EE138B282", "***"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "DF4C45BF43BA614566E1D094195C84B5", "^Simple Collision"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "3B3FCD534F50876F477BBDA88EC702CA", "> Simple Collision mode uses line traces of the simple collision geometry of the level. The particles trace for one channel, selected with Weather Particle Collision Channel. That channel is Visibility by default.\r\n\r\nThe collision traces niagara particles use are queries, so you also need to make sure you have queries enabled on the collision response of your meshes.\r\n\r\nSimple Collision uses various optimizations to minimize the number of collision queries it needs to do. GPU particles take a small number of valid particle paths and reuse them for an amount of time (That time is adjustable with CPU Particle Buffer Length). Even still, it can be a significant CPU cost. Consider Distance Field Collision if this cost is something you want to reduce."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "FC7E7066478CB3FE970A40A58EFBD0DF", "***"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "F1F543D14248BB47C6FCA8BAFCA3BE58", "^Distance Field Collision"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "67BEB17F4229AA0950C041B6BD0BFDF7", "> Distance Field Collision relies purely on GPU emitters, querying the global distance field for its collision. This method comes with upsides and downsides.\r\n\r\nThe main upside is reducing the performance cost on the CPU. Distance field sampling is entirely a GPU operation, and relatively cheap there.\r\n\r\nThe major downside of Distance Field Collision is its lack of flexibility. There is no way for a surface to block particles in this mode without also affecting distance field lighting. And vice versa: to make a mesh allow particles through, you have to disable its effect on distance field lighting.\r\n\r\nNote that to make use of distance field collision, your project must be configured to generate mesh distance fields. Also the distance field collision will only work while the global distance field exists, so it won\'t if that is disabled by the engine scalability."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "59A313104CF53F7D595194BBB66F2331", "***"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "9DC3850B4E514AA15072259E820CFD4F", "If you want to block a space from letting weather particles inside, without any meshes involved, you can use the [UDS_Occlusion_Volume_;udsocclusionvolume] actor, which has a setting to make it block weather particles. Note this is only possible using the Simple Collision mode."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "B9CA5B1647C031FF5071298899913B02", "If you have a moving space you need to block particles where the latency of the particle collision is a problem, for example an interior of a vehicle driven by the player, there is a component you can use in that case. The Weather Particles Kill Sphere can be added to an actor to kill any weather particles inside the sphere with zero latency. Note that this is separate from collision, and is applied by the niagara system uniquely as part of its update process. For this reason, there can never be more than one kill sphere component active at a time. If you need to use them in multiple places, you will need to manage activating and deactivating them to ensure this."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "71613C5F4C4F443B9DA3DD8AC67F220B", "Weather Particle Collision")` |
| `Keywords_8_5ACC585649ABDE1192D0EAB5258A2665` | `TArray` | `("weather particles","collision","rain collision","snow collision","rain inside","snow inside","rain","snow","dust")` |
| `SubCategoryHeading_15_F6EBA06941D30788CC14989999E6C63B` | `bool` | `False` |
| `SuggestedEntries_19_9776F58E45A513F145D90BBE28516AA1` | `TArray` | `("RainParticles","SnowParticles","DustParticles")` |

### Row `WeatherParticleSpawning`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `1` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "7A79C85D492DE2450CBE4CBD43EB2B5D", "When you move the camera around a level, the weather particles will appear to be spawning everywhere, but of course this is just the intended illusion. Weather particles spawn only in a volume around the camera location.\r\n\r\nIn the Shared Particle Settings category, you\'ll find settings to adjust the size and properties of that spawning area.\r\n\r\nMax Spawn Distance and Spawn Distance Distribution control how far from the camera weather particles will spawn in the X and Y axes, and the distribution of particles within that range. Spawn Box Height controls how far above the camera the particles can spawn.\r\n\r\nWorld Spawn Offset and Camera Forward Spawn Offset can be used to move the center of that spawning area relative to the camera position.\r\n\r\nIf you want the weather particles to spawn around a manual location instead of the camera location, you can. In the advanced dropdown of Shared Particle Settings, see the options for the Custom Weather Particle Camera Transform."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "F6E8840140B11726497B1686CBC618C3", "Weather Particle Spawning")` |

### Row `WeatherSeason`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `1` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "7312FE9A4A4DE0139A67F4932EC04C42", "In the Season category, you\'ll find settings for how UDW determines the current [season;season] .\r\n\r\nSeason is a float from 0 to 4, representing the progression from each season to the next, starting with Spring. So for example, 0 is Spring, 0.5 is halfway between Spring and Summer, 2 is Autumn, etc. And 4 is Spring again, completing the cycle.\r\n\r\nIn the Season category, the Season Mode variable determines if the Season is derived from the Date on UDS (entered in Simulation category and incremented with each day that passes). Otherwise, the Season variable is left uncontrolled, for you to set from your own classes as needed for your project. You should do this by calling the Set Season function.\r\n\r\nIf deriving the season from the date, you can use the Season Day Offset to change what date will correspond to what season value. Also note the setting Meteorological Seasons, which sets if the seasons (at offset 0) will represent meteorological seasons or astronomical seasons.\r\n\r\nIf you want to sample the current season in your materials to make effects which respond to the changing season, there are two nodes for that. \"Sample UDW Season\" outputs the 0-1 values for each season. \"Season Color Blend\" takes in 4 color inputs and blends them based on the current season."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "9560FE0D4BEB575B26679EA871F754E7", "Seasons")` |
| `Keywords_8_5ACC585649ABDE1192D0EAB5258A2665` | `TArray` | `("season","spring","summer","fall","autumn","winter")` |

### Row `WeatherSetup`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `1` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "380595234694B233175DDE8CD96E7202", "To set up weather, first make sure you have an Ultra Dynamic Sky actor in your level. The weather system will not work without one. If you haven\'t used Ultra Dynamic Sky yet, you should get started with the Sky section of the documentation instead.\r\n\r\nTo add weather, simply drag an Ultra Dynamic Weather actor from the Blueprints folder into your scene. It will detect Ultra Dynamic Sky on its own and hook everything up.\r\n\r\nBy default, UDW will start with a manual weather state which matches the setup of Cloud Coverage and Fog you already have on UDS. You can select a preset using Weather in Basic Controls to quickly apply different weather types. See the entries below about Weather State for all the other ways weather can be controlled."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "E47DA6C64B7DB08C93FF94A610F53D1C", "Adding Ultra Dynamic Weather to Your Level")` |

### Row `WeatherSounds`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `1` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "A8355CE847E783752D3EDFBCB1DC2D8B", "By default, Ultra Dynamic Weather has sound effects enabled for wind, rain and thunder. From the Sound Effects category, you can disable sound effects, or you can adjust the volume of each as well. The resulting volume of the sounds will scale with these settings as well as the current [weather_state;weatherstate] .\r\n\r\nIf you need to adjust which sounds are turned on at [runtime;runtime] , I\'d recommend leaving the sound effects enabled, and setting their exposed Volume variables at runtime. To toggle all the sound effects at runtime, you can call \"Set Enable Weather Sound Effects\".\r\n\r\nThe Sound Effects category is also where you can adjust how lightning\'s accompanying thunder sound is delayed from the visual effect. By default, the delay is very slight, but you can increase it to represent a realistic speed of sound delay using the setting Close Thunder Delay Per KM.\r\n\r\nAll of the UDW sound effects use a sound class called UDS_Weather. I would recommend adding this class as a child class in your project\'s Sound Effects sound class, so that weather sounds will be affected by mixes applied to general sound effects."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "DE602B064278F970646A449E9DC031AD", "Weather Sound Effects")` |

### Row `What_Determines_WeatherState`

| Field | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Category_12_A3CA532A4207111301CC0DB004E1A0F4` | `int32` | `1` |
| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "A242E9194082BB7FF66E30B49A43EF1B", "The current active [weather_state_;weatherstate] can come from a number of different sources. Here are the places which can inform the current weather state:"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "62CCF06B443B8DD3CC6889A6572579D3", ">- The [weather_settings_preset_;weatherpreset] selected for the Weather variable in Basic Controls.\r\n- The [Change_Weather_;changeweather] function, which transitions from the active weather state to a new preset over a specified amount of time.\r\n- [Random_Weather_Variation;randomweathervariation] , which can change the weather periodically, with the probability of each weather preset affected by the current [season;season] .\r\n- The [Manual_Weather_State_;manualweatherstate] values, in the Manual Weather State category, used in place of the Weather variable when nothing is selected for it. Individual values from the manual weather state can also be applied as overrides, having an effect no matter what is currently contributing to the weather state.\r\n- [Weather_Override_Volumes;weatheroverridevolume] . This is a separate actor which can be placed into the level to apply weather that is specific to a region of any shape.\r\n- [Radial_Storms;radialstorm] . This actor applies weather in a circular region, with its own additional effects to render the weather/clouds so they are visible from outside the storm."),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "4C0E83A64528E76612DE2DA9BCEFCAA8", "See the entries specific to each of these for more information about how to make use of them."))` |
| `EntryTitle_4_4B2C1546415E1329EC06F8B28CB05DF9` | `FText` | `NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "3D48D3774A2067C10D2D90ABEC93FC04", "What Determines the Weather State?")` |

These are the values which comprise the weather state:"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "12994BEB4446C86E50721392D8C4033A", ">- Cloud Coverage\r\n- Fog\r\n- Wind Intensity\r\n- Rain\r\n- Snow\r\n- Dust\r\n- Thunder/Lightning"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "E40A3D7341C64A18304862BB0C258E10", "There\'s also the [material_state;materialstate] , which controls the state of the material effects specifically:"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "98DBB7A444B875308919D5AB8167AE8F", ">- Material Snow Coverage\r\n- Material Wetness\r\n- Material Dust Coverage"),NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "9783F18149F7FDC6E40BEF85B367A4EC", "These are part of the weather state, but at [runtime_;runtime] the visible material state is not always derived directly from the values in the weather state. You can read more about the specifics of this in the section on material effects."))` |

### Row `WindActor`

This uses random noise to vary the direction of the wind at [runtime._;runtime] This variation is centered around the Wind Direction selected in Basic Controls.\r\n\r\nWeather Override Volumes can also override wind direction as well. If Apply Wind Direction is true on a WOV, the wind direction setting below will be used as the player enters the volume."))` |

| `EntryText_13_1F188F814F7F03D55DA1ED8DF4CC1347` | `TArray` | `(NSLOCTEXT("[62584B454EB15A1F28B05A88048C49F4]", "177F192A4EFC79F86EFE589B13E8232E", "If you have objects which simulate physics, and you want them to be able to be pushed by the current wind on UDW, there is a component included for that. It\'s the Wind Physics Force component.\r\n\r\nJust add this component as a child of any primitive component which simulates physics. At [runtime;runtime] , the component will query the current wind state on UDW and do line traces to see how exposed to wind the component is.\r\n\r\nYou can adjust the strength of the wind\'s physical force, as well as other specifics of how the component behaves, from its exposed settings."))` |
